title: The SIRMOS mission concept: a space-based near-IR spectroscopic survey of 100 million galaxies in the Euclid Wide Survey footprint
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables, presented at SPIE Space Telescopes and Instrumentation 2026: Optical, Infrared, and Millimeter Wave (August 2026)
summary:
SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy.
  To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $μ$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.

title: A High Precision Metacalibration Response Correction
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures
summary: In Metacalibration the shear response of a weak lensing measurement is estimated by applying an artificial shear to the image, but the shear operation imprints a spin-2 modulation on the image noise power, which biases the measured response. The standard fix adds a sheared noise field that symmetrizes the anisotropy, at the cost of doubling the noise variance ($\sqrt2$ in the noise). The fusion correction presented in this note reaches the same unbiased response while adding only the minimum power needed. It measures the noise power transfer by passing an impulse through the Metacal process, forms the common-level azimuthal deficit that equalizes the spin-2 ($m{=}2$) and spin-6 ($m{=}6$) modulations across the metacal types, and adds just that deficit by filtering the rotated noise field. The fusion correction raises the per-pixel noise by only $\sim2\%$ for a round PSF (versus $\sqrt2$ for the standard correction), rising toward the $\sqrt2$ level only for highly elliptical PSFs.

title: ASTRA: An Autonomous Framework for Physics-Validated Analysis and Hypothesis Generation in Astrophysics
comment: 27 pages - MNRAS - RAS Techniques and Instruments - accepted - in press
summary: We present ASTRA, an autonomous framework for physics-validated analysis and hypothesis generation in astrophysics without per-step human intervention. It integrates dimensional analysis, structural causal models, Bayesian evidence computation, and multi-wavelength data fusion in a single automated workflow. Five test cases on real observational data recover known results: Herschel filament scaling, Chandra Deep Field South cross-matching, SDSS galaxy correlations, Gaia causal inference, and Bayesian virial model selection. A sixth case runs unsupervised on synthetic galaxy data. The main sequence and mass-metallicity relation are recovered, and the outlier detector, with a false-discovery-rate threshold and no contamination parameter, recovers the blind injected fraction on ten sealed datasets (purity > 0.99) and flags nothing on the 3,000-galaxy sample. A knowledge-isolation ablation shows pattern detection and physical validation are invariant to removal of domain knowledge, which affects only interpretation. In a direct comparison, agentic-LLM and pure-ML baselines match the statistical fitting but not the physics-validation stage. They rarely derive the equilibrium benchmark, split evenly on the physical verdict, and adopt a supplied erroneous benchmark in all six trap runs, an astrophysics-specific fine-tuned model completes zero of six runs. On live SDSS DR16 data it flags 197 of 4,999 galaxies at a data-determined threshold, ranked extremes classifiable from withheld spectroscopy. These are recovery validations and capability demonstrations rather than discoveries, with hypothesis generation demonstrated qualitatively.

title: Propulsion Systems for a Starshade Rendezvous Mission with the Habitable World Observatory
comment: 39 pages, 11 figure, 4 tables. Accepted for publication on JATIS
summary: We assess how propulsion and operational constraints affect exo-Earth characterization with a starshade rendezvous mission for a Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO)-like telescope at Sun-Earth L2. Using end-to-end Monte Carlo simulations with EXOSIMS, we model a 60 m starshade for visible-band spectroscopy (500-1000 nm) and a 35 m starshade for near-ultraviolet characterization (250-550 nm). For the 60 m design, we compare AEPS Hall, NEXT ion, and Starlink-class Hall thrusters and examine sensitivity to propellant capacity, the fraction of each retargeting slew spent accelerating and decelerating, and on-orbit refueling. With 1000-3000 kg of initial propellant and no refueling, NEXT provides the highest characterization yield: 9-13% more characterizations than AEPS and 13-16% more than the Starlink-class option. Its higher specific impulse enables more retargeting slews per kilogram of propellant. With refueling, yields converge across thruster choices to about 120 cumulative characterizations over 10 years, while propulsion choice mainly affects the number of refueling events. For the 35 m starshade with AEPS, yields are less sensitive to fuel and are dominated by mission duration and geometric accessibility. Increasing the minimum solar keepout angle from 40 to 50 degrees has little effect on yield; increases from 50 to 65 degrees have a modest effect, while angles above 65 degrees rapidly reduce yield, with severe degradation near 80 degrees. These results distinguish fuel-limited and time- or keepout-limited regimes and guide propulsion selection, tank sizing, refueling policy, and keepout constraints for HWO starshade missions.

title: CROMA: a GPU-accelerated Fokker--Planck solver for modeling non-thermal emission in post-processing cosmological simulations
comment: 15 pages, submitted to Astronomy & Computing
summary: Numerical modeling of cosmic-ray (CR) spectra and the resulting non-thermal emission is important for understanding the physical mechanisms of CR acceleration and transport in astrophysical environments. Galaxy clusters and cosmic filaments provide particularly important environments for studying these processes, where shocks, turbulence, magnetic fields, and CRs jointly shape diffuse synchrotron emission. Spectrally resolved modeling of CRs, including cooling, re-acceleration, and hadronic interactions, requires solving time-dependent Fokker--Planck (FP) equations. An increasing number of studies employ FP solvers coupled with magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations to follow the evolution of CRs in dynamically evolving environments. We present a new C/C++-based FP solver with GPU acceleration for post-processing outputs from cosmological MHD simulations. The code evolves CR proton and electron spectra along Lagrangian tracer trajectories and consistently includes re-acceleration and secondary-particle production processes. With the Chang--Cooper finite-difference scheme, the FP equation for each tracer is reduced to an independent tridiagonal system, which is solved on NVIDIA GPUs using a CUDA implementation of the parallel cyclic reduction (PCR) algorithm. The code uses sub-stepping between tracer snapshots, with the timestep constrained by the relevant CR cooling or re-acceleration timescale, and a batching algorithm that groups tracers with similar sub-stepping patterns for efficient execution. We find that the GPU acceleration increases the per-node throughput by a factor of $\approx$10 on the Leonardo Booster system operated by CINECA. The fast FP solver is useful for high-resolution simulations dedicated to comparison with next-generation radio observations and future multi-messenger applications combining radio, gamma-ray, and high-energy neutrino observations.

title: The Stellar Populations of Resolved Galaxies
comment: Invited Review. Accepted for publication in Physics Reports. 221 pages (115 main text, 46 appendices, 60 references), 36 figures. Movie of Fig. 7 at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23627360
summary: The study of galaxies outside the Milky Way using observations of resolved stellar populations has experienced extraordinary growth over the past two decades. There now exist panchromatic photometry and precise astrometry for hundreds of millions of individually resolved stars in hundreds of galaxies that span $\sim10^9$ in luminosity, $\sim10^3$ in metallicity, and sample a wide range of environments. Here, we review advances in extragalactic astronomy enabled by resolved stellar population imaging. We summarize major observational programs and focus on four interconnected science areas: the star formation histories of galaxies, 'bursty' star formation, the stellar initial mass function, and the orbital histories of Local Group galaxies. We review the literature in each area, synthesize key findings, identify emerging trends, and discuss how new and future facilities (e.g., JWST, LSST, Euclid, Roman, CSST, ELTs, HWO) will enable further progress. Finally, we highlight shortcomings in current datasets and discuss promising directions for new areas of investigation.

title: Field-level modeling of halo and galaxy alignments
comment: 31+11 pages, 13+8 figures
summary: We develop an effective field theory (EFT) of intrinsic alignments at the level of spin-2 field fluctuations of large-scale structure tracers, such as the shapes of galaxies and dark matter halos. Our perturbative model includes the non-linear treatment of the Zel'dovich displacement, and contains all necessary shape operators through the third order. We apply our field-level model to the full 3D distribution of galaxy shapes, whose sky projections are a known contaminant of cosmic shear measurements. Our field-level EFT model achieves a better description of the helicity fields of dark matter halo shapes than the standard non-linear alignment (NLA) and tidal torquing + tidal alignment (TATT) models in the literature, as evidenced by improved correlations with the simulations' initial conditions. We perform precision measurements of field-level bias parameters by means of a generalized least-squares problem, for which we derive an optimal estimator and analytic covariance matrices. We measure the full set of linear, quadratic, and cubic shape bias coefficients as a function of halo mass in the $\texttt{Quijote}$ N-body simulations. We then study the intrinsic alignments of galaxies in the $\texttt{FLAMINGO}$ hydrodynamical simulation, focusing on observationally relevant samples: spirals, ellipticals, luminous red galaxies (LRG) and emission-line galaxies (ELG). We detect linear and nonlinear alignment coefficients at high significance for LRG, spiral and elliptical galaxies. We also find evidence for non-zero density-weighted tidal bias coefficient of the simulated ELG. This work supports the notion that EFT-based models of alignments will be paramount in optimally extracting constraints from future shape correlations, and lays the foundation for the development of simulation-based priors for future galaxy shape samples.

title: The [Y/Mg] chemical clock and the stellar ages of solar-type stars in the solar neighbourhood
comment: Published in the proceedings of the International Astronomical Union
summary: Stellar ages are an important parameter for studying the chemical evolution of the Galaxy. To improve age estimates, various complementary methods to the conventional isochrone-fitting method have been implemented in the last decade. The [Y/Mg] ratio has been proposed as a chemical clock for solar-metallicity stars, due to its strong dependence on stellar age. In this work, we study the behaviour of the abundance ratio [Y/Mg] in metal-poor stars, along with other solar-type disk stars, as a function of stellar age determined through isochrones. The analysis is based on the line-by-line differential technique, applied to a sample covering a wide metallicity range ($-$0.70 $\leq$ [Fe/H] $<$ +0.34), using high-resolution (R = 115,000) and high S/N spectra (= 270 - 1000) taken with the HARPS spectrograph at the ESO La Silla Observatory. We find that the stellar sample follows a metallicity-dependent [Y/Mg]-Age relation.

title: A Model to Map Brown Dwarf Companions to White Dwarfs in Partial Secondary Eclipse
comment: Submitted to The Open Journal of Astrophysics via arXiv
summary: Eclipse mapping is a well-established technique for constraining the spatial emission of hot Jupiter exoplanets. Brown dwarfs in ultra-short orbits around white dwarfs are an analog to hot Jupiters that can only ever be eclipsed within a limited range of latitudes. We adapt the eigenmapping method to disentangle the signals from the ever- and never-occulted regions. The result of this signal separation is a super-position of map structures, yielding sharp boundaries at the occultation region. We introduce a model that penalizes the harmonic complexity of the model map with Tikhonov regularization, whose parameters are tuned to reproduce the fit quality of the eigenmapping model. We use JWST NIRSpec/PRISM full-orbit observations of the eclipsing WD 1202-024 system as a template to construct and run injection-recovery tests on simulated light curves, isolating both latitudinal structures as well as emission from a physically-realistic general circulation model (GCM). In the latter, the narrow equatorial jet driven by the BD's rapid rotation manifests as an eclipse depth asymmetry, which our model reproduces as a latitude-dependent phase offset. Such a model, however, is only statistically preferred at approximately $3 \times$ the signal-to-noise ratio of the JWST data. When fitting to the actual JWST data of WD 1202, the full-phase eigenbasis model is statistically preferred. However, the resulting model map of WD 1202 B does not resemble the GCM predictions, with a concentrated day-side hotspot at the sub-stellar point with an angular size $\approx 15^\circ$. Interpreting this result more carefully requires follow-up work to disentangle systematics from true emission signals. This model framework provides a means to detect emission features from these rare types of eclipses, and ultimately to test predictions of models of atmospheric circulation across hot Jupiters and their BD analogs.

title: The Great Chat in the Sky: Aligning Exotic Astronomical Data to Language with AstroBridge
summary: Astronomical observations include images, spectra, and light curves, while the scientific literature describes these objects in natural language. We present AstroBridge, a framework that connects these observations to an LLM through a literature-assisted caption generation pipeline. We used catalog metadata to match observations with scientific texts that describe the same objects. A vision-language model generates descriptive captions from representations of observations, matched passages, and available metadata, creating observation-caption pairs without manual captioning. We train AstroBridge to predict captions directly from raw observations. Modality-specific frozen encoders extract representations that a shared, trainable fusion network aligns with the embedding space of an LLM. In caption-based evaluation of spectra, AstroBridge achieves 91.5% accuracy in distinguishing quasars from galaxies, compared to 69.0% from the base model prior to fine-tuning. Limitations remain in galaxy morphology, classification of minority supernova classes, and the factual quality of generated captions. We believe that AstroBridge's framework is a step towards the goal of aligning the totality of astronomy's diverse, exotic data through the lingua franca of text.

title: Dynamical constraints on the companion mass from pulsar timing and cyclotron line confirmation in the SFXT IGR J16418-4532
comment: 9 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Supergiant Fast X-ray Transients (SFXTs) show extreme X-ray variability on timescales of minutes to hours, driven by accretion processes that remain poorly understood. IGR J16418-4532 is an intermediate SFXT with detected X-ray pulsations and a candidate cyclotron line, making it a key system for probing neutron-star accretion and magnetic fields in this class. We analysed a 148 ks NuSTAR observation and archival RXTE observations, using epoch folding to search for pulsations while correcting photon arrival times for a range of trial $a_x \sin i$ values, and performed phase-averaged spectroscopy with several continuum models. We detect coherent pulsations at $P_{\rm spin} = 1208.67 \pm 0.04$ s (NuSTAR) and $1209.4178 \pm 0.0084$ s (RXTE/PCA). The pulse detection depends clearly on the assumed projected semi-major axis and is most significant for $a_x \sin i = 55.1 \pm 3.5$ lt-s (NuSTAR) and $51.3 \pm 2.6$ lt-s (RXTE/PCA). Sliding-window pulse profiles show the orbital delay in the uncorrected data, which is fully removed after orbital correction. The inferred orbital parameters constrain the companion mass and radius to $\sim$12-18 $M_\odot$ and $\sim$13-16 $R_\odot$. This is the first constraint on the binary mass function of an SFXT obtained from the orbital motion of the neutron star. The spectrum shows a robust cyclotron absorption line at $\sim$50 keV, independent of the continuum model, implying $B \approx 5 \times 10^{12}$ G. Optimising pulse detection with trial $a_x \sin i$ corrections, rather than modelling pulse arrival-time delays, offers a route to dynamical mass measurements in other SFXTs whose variable pulse profiles limit conventional timing techniques.

title: Detection of star formation in a near-pristine pocket of the Universe
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
summary: We detect two high-confidence star-forming sources in the environment of a chemically near-pristine ([Fe/H] $<-3.66~;2σ)$ Damped Ly$α$ system (DLA) using Keck/KCWI. These are found via the hydrogen Ly$α$ emission line at $Δv=-1200$ kms$^{-1}$ (LAE1) and $Δv = -200$ kms$^{-1}$ (LAE2) relative to the DLA redshift ($z_{\rm abs} = 3.078$) at an impact parameter of $b=66$ physical kpc and $b=137$ physical kpc. We measure Ly$α$ fluxes of $F(\rm Lyα)_{\rm LAE1} =4.4\pm 0.7\times10^{-18}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}$ and $F(\rm Lyα)_{\rm LAE2} =3.8\pm 0.9\times10^{-18}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}$. This marks the first detection of star formation in the environment of a chemically near-pristine DLA. We use red channel Keck/KCRM data to place limits on the associated He II 1640 A emission flux of these sources, $F(\rm He\,II)<3.8\times10^{-19}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}~(3σ)$ and $F(\rm He\,II) <3.7\times10^{-19}~\rm erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}~(3σ)$. The weak and narrow properties of the Ly$α$ emission, combined with the inferred position on the mass-metallicity relation, suggest a metal-paucity of these galaxies. Future rest-frame optical observations are required to pin down the metallicity of LAE1 and LAE2 and test if chemically near-pristine DLAs can be used as a signpost to search for primitive, metal-poor galaxies 2 Gyrs after the Big Bang.

title: Two-dimensional galaxy cluster shapes using lensing data: a simulated analysis
comment: submitted to A&A, 16 pages, 9 figures; comments are welcome
summary: Context. Cluster morphology reflects assembly history and dynamical state. High-resolution weak lensing can reveal departures from spherical symmetry, but its ability to recover two-dimensional shapes remains less explored. Aims. We assess how reliably weak lensing recovers projected cluster morphology and its dependence on orientation and dynamical state. We also compare large-scale weak-lensing morphology with that traced by strong lensing near the cluster centre. Methods. We study three clusters at $z=0.22$ from The Three Hundred Project, representing relaxed, mildly disturbed and unrelaxed systems. For each, we consider three random projections and three along the principal axes of the mass tensor. For each projection, we generate 128 weak-lensing catalogues with a source density of 30 arcmin$^{-2}$ and intrinsic ellipticity dispersion $σ_ε=0.3$. We constrain mass and concentration from one-dimensional NFW and BMO fits, then recover ellipticity, position angle and centre using a two-dimensional elliptical NFW model. We also measure morphology from true convergence maps, Kaiser \& Squires reconstructions and strong-lensing tangential critical lines. Results. Recovered parameters depend on orientation and dynamical state. The relaxed cluster has similar inner and large-scale shapes, whereas disturbed systems appear more elliptical centrally. Two-dimensional weak-lensing modelling recovers the projected mass orientation despite source sampling and shape noise. Kaiser \& Squires reconstructions recover the position angle well but favour rounder mass distributions. Centroid offsets are larger in unrelaxed systems. Conclusions. Combining weak- and strong-lensing morphology probes cluster structure across physical scales and offers a promising way to investigate morphology and dynamical state.

title: An intermediate-mass stripped star with a dark companion in the Small Magellanic Cloud
comment: 22 pages, 13 figures, submitted to PASP
summary: We present discovery of SMASH J004005$-$733351, an intermediate-mass stripped helium star in the Small Magellanic Cloud with a dark companion. The system was identified in a new optical color-selected survey for stripped stars and confirmed through spectroscopic follow-up. We measure an orbital period of $P_{\rm orb}=19.95\pm 0.002$ hours and a radial-velocity semi-amplitude of $K=91.7 ^{+3.2}_{-3.1}\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$. Simultaneous modeling of the optical spectrum and ultraviolet-to-optical spectral energy distribution yields a stripped star evolutionary mass $M_{\rm stripped} = 3.84 \pm 0.54\,M_\odot$, temperature $T_{\rm eff} = 68.3 \pm 6.4$ kK, surface gravity $\log g= 4.76 \pm 0.12$, luminosity $\log(L/L_\odot)= 4.28 \pm 0.13$, radius $R= 0.99 \pm 0.09\,R_\odot$, and an unusually high surface hydrogen abundance of $X_{\rm H, s}=0.63 \pm 0.04$. The companion is undetected spectroscopically, and the orbital solution and stripped-star evolutionary mass imply a minimum companion mass of $M_2 \gtrsim 1.2\,M_\odot$. The absence of photometric variability from irradiation rules out a main-sequence companion. The companion is most likely a neutron star (NS), although a massive white dwarf or low-mass stripped star cannot be fully excluded. Binary evolution models predict that the stripped star will refill its Roche lobe after core helium exhaustion, likely producing a stripped or ultra-stripped supernova and ultimately a double NS binary if the system survives. SMASH J004005$-$733351 is among the first known stripped stars with a compact object companion. The system provides a new empirical benchmark for the late stages of binary interaction that lead to (ultra-)stripped supernovae and double NS binaries.

authors: for the PLATO Stellar Variability Working Group
title: Measuring masses of transiting Earth-like planets: first insights from the PLATO RV data challenge
summary:
The PLATO Stellar Variability Mitigation Working Group designed a radial-velocity (RV) data challenge to assess the precision and accuracy achievable on RV semi-amplitudes in the context of the future PLATO follow-up.
  Using Sun-as-a-star observations obtained with HARPS-N, we generated three multi-planet systems with realistic sampling, an effective signal-to-noise ratio of S/N ~ 450, an exposure time of 15 minutes, and a total of approximately 1000 observations. The resulting data set is publicly available and can serve as a benchmark for the community to test and compare RV analysis methods. Eight independent teams participated in the challenge, aiming to recover the semi-amplitudes of both transiting and non-transiting planets.
  A meta-analysis of the submitted results shows that, with current data analysis methods, HARPS-N-like stability and the observing strategy studied in this paper, achieving a precision on semi-amplitudes better than 10% for habitable-zone signals around a solar-type star is challenging, and is typically limited to planets with masses of approximately 8-10 Earth masses. This performance is expected to improve for K dwarfs, where planets down to approximately 2-5 Earth masses may be characterized at a similar level of precision.
  Finally, based on the results of this challenge and the occurrence of false positives, we derive an empirical detection threshold for RV surveys, which can be used to distinguish robust planetary detections from candidates.

title: Overview And Present Status Of The 4-m International Liquid Mirror Telescope (ILMT)
summary: The International Liquid Mirror Telescope (ILMT) is an inexpensive optical instrument with a diameter of 4 metres, entirely dedicated to astronomical surveys. Its scientific programmes include the detection and study of transients, variable objects, asteroids, comets, low surface brightness galaxies, space debris, etc. The telescope achieved its first light on 29 April 2022 and was officially inaugurated on 21 March 2023. It has been operating regularly since October 2023 and continuously observes the sky passing through the zenith using the SDSS $g^{\prime}$, $r^{\prime}$, and $i^{\prime}$ filters in a narrow band of the sky ($22.3^{\prime}$) centred around the equatorial declination of $+29°21^{\prime}41^{\prime \prime}$. Here we report on the astrometric and photometric performance of the ILMT and summarise the main results obtained since the BINA3 workshop. A great way to raise public awareness is to build a scale model of a liquid mirror telescope. General guidelines for doing so are provided.

title: Reconstruction of very inclined air showers with radio data and application to the first GRANDProto300 cosmic-ray candidates
comment: Presented at the 60th Rencontres de Moriond on Very High Energy Phenomena in the Universe (Moriond VHEPU 2026). 4 pages, 5 figures
summary: Radio detection of very inclined extensive air showers (EAS) offers a promising way to study ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and neutrinos above $10^{17}$ eV. We present a method to reconstruct the arrival direction and energy of EAS with zenith angles above $60^\circ$, applicable in principle to upward-going neutrino-induced showers. The approach combines a point-source-like description of the radio wavefront with the Angular Distribution Function (ADF), a phenomenological model describing the angular pattern of electric field amplitudes in the 50-200 MHz band. On realistic cosmic-ray simulations, we achieve better than $0.07^\circ$ resolution on arrival direction and ~15\% on primary energy. Applied directly to voltage traces, this method allows efficient cosmic-ray selection with accurate direction reconstruction and first-order energy estimation. We illustrate the method on the first cosmic-ray candidates detected by the GRANDProto300 prototype of GRAND, validating its detection principle and paving the way for high-precision neutrino searches.

title: What sets the star-formation rate in the Milky Way? I. A multi-scale view of the star-formation rate
comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, submitted to A&A
summary:
Context. The star-formation rate (SFR) is one of the key quantities that characterizes the star formation process and has been extensively investigated both observationally and theoretically.
  Aims. We aim to provide a coherent multi-scale view of star formation by connecting Galactic-scale conditions (kpc) to the properties of individual star-forming clumps at sub-parsec scales.
  Methods. We perform a set of numerical simulations with large-scale turbulent forcing designed to reproduce physical conditions typical of the solar neighbourhood. Using adaptive zooming down to 0.03 pc, we obtain a population of star-forming clumps that is analyzed and compared with observational catalogues in a companion paper.
  Results. For column densities and velocity dispersions consistent with Galactic values, the resulting SFR is close to the rate inferred for the Milky Way. Comparing this value with the SFR expected from pure free-fall collapse shows that turbulence provides multiscale support that lowers the SFR by more than an order of magnitude. Additional regulation by stellar feedback, including ionizing radiation and protostellar outflows, likely reduces the SFR by an additional factor of 3-10. Comparisons with observations across multiple spatial scales show good overall agreement with this model.
  Conclusions. These results support a picture in which turbulence plays a central role in regulating star formation in the Milky Way. In combination with stellar feedback, it limits the star formation efficiency to only a few percent.
  Key words. stars: formation -- ISM: clouds -- physical processes: turbulence

title: Does the Escape Fraction Prescription Shape Reionization History and Morphology?
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to ApJ. Comments are welcome
summary: The escape fraction of ionizing photons, $f_{\rm esc}$, is one of the least constrained quantities of the Epoch of Reionization (EoR), and the opacity of the intergalactic medium prevents its direct measurement at high redshifts. We constrain three power-law parameterizations, $f_{\rm esc}(z)$, $f_{\rm esc}(M_{\rm h})$, and $f_{\rm esc}(z, M_{\rm h})$, against JWST UV luminosity functions and EoR observables (the ionizing emissivity, the neutral hydrogen fraction, and the Thomson optical depth) using Markov Chain Monte Carlo, with priors that allow $f_{\rm esc}$ to either increase or decrease with redshift and halo mass. We then propagate the best-fit models into the semi-numerical simulation SimFast21 and compare their ionization morphology and 21 cm power spectra with those of a constant-$f_{\rm esc}$ model. All models reproduce the observations with nearly identical global reionization histories. The data favor an escape fraction that decreases with increasing redshift, from $\approx 0.8$ at $z = 5$ to $\approx 0.35$ at $z = 15$. The halo-mass-only model prefers $f_{\rm esc}$ increasing with halo mass, but this trend acts as a proxy for redshift evolution. When we vary both dependencies jointly, the data prefer a mass-independent $f_{\rm esc}$. At matched global neutral fraction, the ionization morphology is closely similar for all four prescriptions, and the 21 cm power spectra agree to within $\approx 10\%$. These results suggest that, once calibrated against the same observations, the details of the $f_{\rm esc}$ prescription, which are set by the physics of the interstellar medium, largely average out in both the global observables and the 21 cm power spectrum. Distinguishing them may require statistics beyond the power spectrum, such as sightline statistics of the Ly$α$ and 21 cm forests, or forecasts that exploit their small differences in reionization timing.

title: The evolutionary history of ultra-compact accreting binaries. II. HST spectroscopy of two eclipsing AM CVn stars
comment: 15 pages, 11 figures; submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: AM CVn stars are ultra-compact binaries in which a white dwarf (WD) accretes helium-rich material from a hydrogen-deficient donor. They are promising mHz gravitational-wave sources and potential progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. However, their evolutionary pathways remain uncertain. Three formation channels have been proposed: the WD, helium star, and cataclysmic variable channels. We aim to determine the atmospheric chemical composition of the underlying accreting WDs in two eclipsing AM CVn systems, YZ LMi and ZTF J0407-00, in order to constrain their formation channels. Using ultraviolet spectra obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope, we modelled the atmospheres of the accreting WDs, whose surface compositions are enriched by material transferred from the donor and therefore trace the donor's composition. In particular, the nitrogen-to-carbon abundance ratio provides a diagnostic of the donor's nuclear burning history and hence of the system's formation channel. We measure effective temperatures Teff = 24400 $\pm$ 1500 K and surface gravities logg = 8.36 $\pm$ 0.05 for YZ LMi, and Teff = 29900 $\pm$ 2200 K and logg = 8.37 $\pm$ 0.05 for ZTF J0407-00. The inferred masses of the two WDs are 0.84 $\pm$ 0.10 and 0.86 $\pm$ 0.12 solar masses, respectively. Carbon is not detected in either system, yielding lower limits on the nitrogen-to-carbon mass ratio of N/C > 117 and N/C > 185. We increase from one to three the number of AM CVn systems whose accreting WDs and chemical abundances have been analysed using detailed UV atmosphere models. The high N/C ratios rule out the helium star formation channel for both systems. The WD channel is favoured by the absence of detectable hydrogen at all observed wavelengths, although the evolved cataclysmic variable channel cannot be conclusively excluded.

title: Retention of primordial atmospheres through giant impacts
comment: 34 pages, 6 main figures and 2 extended figures. Published in Nature Astronomy
summary: Rocky planets the size of Earth or larger are expected to undergo one or more giant impacts during the final stages of their formation. Some of these collisions occur after protoplanetary disk dissipation, potentially driving the loss of primordial hydrogen-rich atmospheres through elevated surface temperatures. However, whether giant impacts promote atmospheric loss or retention remains unclear because they both heat planetary interiors and increase atmospheric gravitational binding. Here we model the evolution of rocky planets after their largest post-disk giant impact, accounting self-consistently for the concurrent increase in gravitational binding energy and mantle thermal energy. Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature. Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactor's metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth. Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention. Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth. By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths.

title: FLITS: an interactive, reproducible workbench for fast radio burst analysis
comment: 6 pages. Code: https://github.com/DirkKuiper/flits ; documentation: https://dirkkuiper.github.io/flits/ ; software archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23596340
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief flashes of radio emission whose time, frequency, and polarization structure constrain their sources and propagation environments. FLITS (Fast-Look Interactive Transient Suite) is an open-source Python package with a browser interface for analysing detected bursts. It combines data inspection, interference mitigation, measurement, and modelling, including fits of the fitburst burst model, in a shared session, and reads SIGPROC filterbank, PSRFITS, and CHIME/FRB HDF5 data. The same routines measure larger samples from the command line and flag bursts whose automatic selections need checking. Trial dispersion measures can be scored by signal-to-noise, by burst structure, or with a smoothed-structure metric that also reports the range of dispersion measures consistent with the best one. Portable session files retain the selected data regions, excluded channels, calibration inputs, available results, input-data checksum, and software provenance, and supported measurements can be replayed from the command line and compared with their saved values. Uncertainty labels identify missing calibration information. A public reference workflow provides downloadable data and numerical checks.

title: Three-flavor neutrino Boltzmann transport and flavor instabilities in long-lived neutron-star merger remnants
summary: Binary neutron-star (BNS) mergers are multimessenger sources whose kilonova emission and nucleosynthesis depend sensitively on neutrino microphysics and flavor conversion. Most BNS merger simulations assume $μ$-$τ$ neutrino degeneracy in a two-flavor treatment. We investigate the fast flavor instability (FFI) and the collisional flavor instability (CFI) in long-lived BNS merger remnants using axisymmetric general-relativistic three-flavor Boltzmann neutrino transport with a comprehensive treatment of muons and muonic interactions, following a handoff from 3D grey moment-based simulations. Our simulations largely reproduce the parent 3D simulations, recovering trapped weak equilibrium in the core, muonic non-equilibrium in the semitransparent outer disk due to prolonged demuonization, and cold weak equilibrium in transparent regions. Linear stability analysis reveals strong and widespread CFI in all three flavor sectors, including narrow resonance-like structures. Muonic interactions reshape the FFI distribution, shifting the $eτ$-sector instability toward denser disk regions compared with the extended FFI outside the disk in the two-flavor model, while disk demuonization produces a strong $ν_μ$ excess and one-sided muon-lepton-number angular distributions that suppress FFI in the $eμ$ and $μτ$ sectors. Local three-flavor quantum kinetic equation (QKE) calculations reveal nonlinear coupling among flavor sectors that excites coherence even in an initially stable sector. Diagonal collisional repopulation is decisive for the nonlinear evolution and asymptotic flavor populations, and neglecting it overestimates flavor equilibration. We establish the necessity of three-flavor transport from both classical and quantum perspectives, and underscore the importance of consistently coupling flavor conversion with diagonal collisional repopulation in future CFI subgrid models.

title: Dependence of Merger-driven Star Formation and Gas-phase Metallicity Evolution on Merger Type and Stellar Mass
comment: 24 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Galaxy mergers play a fundamental role in driving gas inflows, altering star formation, and redistributing metals, yet how these processes depend on merger type, merger stage, and progenitor galaxy properties remains incompletely understood. In this work, we investigate the resolved impact of mergers on star formation rate (SFR) and gas-phase metallicity using MaNGA integral-field spectroscopy and the MaNGA Galaxy Merger Catalog of Comerford et al. (2024). By comparing merger galaxies to matched controls, we quantify local offsets in SFR and metallicity as functions of merger type, merger stage, stellar mass, and galactocentric radius. We find that major mergers generally exhibit stronger SFR enhancement and greater metallicity dilution than minor mergers. In major mergers, SFR enhancement is often spatially extended, whereas in minor mergers it is weaker and more centrally concentrated. The SFR response in major mergers varies non-monotonically with merger stage, with stronger enhancement in the early (first-passage) and post-coalescence stages and weaker enhancement in the late (between-passage) stage. Metallicity dilution is generally strongest in early-stage major mergers and weaker at later stages, although this stage dependence is not monotonic across all stellar-mass bins. We also find stellar-mass dependence that lower-mass systems show stronger metallicity dilution in both major and minor mergers, while the strongest SFR enhancement occurs in intermediate- and high-mass major mergers. These results show that the resolved star formation and metallicity responses depend jointly on merger type, merger stage, and stellar mass and exhibit different behaviors across the merger sequence.

title: ECH0EZ: Estimating the Hubble constant with ZTF SN Ia DR2
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures (+ appendix)
summary: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are instrumental for a precise measurement of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) from the local distance ladder, yet the data used hitherto for this purpose are inhomogeneous and subject to severe selection effects. We present the first, preliminary, cosmological analysis of 772 SNe Ia from the Zwicky Transient Facility's second data release: an untargeted single-telescope sample whose volume-limited subset (z<0.06) is largely free of Malmquist bias. We correct the public data for known instrumental and calibration biases and the redshifts for peculiar motions. Using the 42 SH0ES calibrators (their host distances computed from Cepheids and geometric anchors) and a Bayesian hierarchical model of SN Ia standardisation, dust extinction, redshift and calibration uncertainties, we infer $H_0 = (71.6 \pm 1.5)$ km/s/Mpc after marginalising over deceleration with a flat prior (or $(72.3 \pm 1.1)$ km/s/Mpc if a prior on matter density from Pantheon+ is imposed), with the uncertainty dominated by the number of calibrators. We demonstrate robustness to the choice of light-curve and Milky Way dust models and to extensions of the model to include peculiar-velocity correlations, a host-mass step, and two stretch populations. These results are in agreement with previous distance-ladder measurements and $2.7σ$ ($4.1σ$) away from the value obtained from Planck data, suggesting that the resolution of the Hubble tension lies outside of SNe Ia---or the distance ladder entirely.

title: DUETS II - Red giant asteroseismic binaries. Binary confirmation and prospects for double-seismic model inference
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics. 14 main pages (9 appendix), 8 main figures (9 appendix), 3 main tables (5 appendix)
summary: Red giants displaying solar-like oscillations allow precise stellar properties to be derived. Asteroseismic binaries (ABs), which are gravitationally bound systems where both stars show detectable oscillations, can provide constraints on the interior of two coeval stars, allowing us to model them jointly and potentially obtain constraints unavailable from either star individually. This makes ABs potential laboratories for calibrating stellar evolution theory. In this context, AB candidates (ABCs) are systems showing two oscillators, which are as of yet not confirmed as gravitationally bound. We aimed to confirm ABCs and other red giant binary candidates, as well as demonstrate the advantages of AB modeling inference. We obtained spectroscopic indicators of binarity for 60 oscillating red giants that have photometric (33 stars) and/or asteroseismic (38) indications of binarity. We confirm 12 of our 60 targets as spectroscopic binaries, 8 of which are ABs as well. Cross-matching with Gaia DR3 and APOGEE DR17, we identify a further 9 likely binaries, at least 6 of which are also ABCs. We then investigated the impact of simultaneously modeling the oscillation modes of both oscillators of an AB. We inferred stellar properties for; one binary of extra-Galactic origin containing one detectable red-giant-branch (RGB) oscillator; one AB with RGB oscillators; and two ABCs with RGB oscillators. We find that the mode frequencies of the two ABCs and the confirmed AB are well-described with a coeval modeling of the stellar components. We demonstrate that the simultaneous modeling of ABs with two RGB stars can be used to infer the stellar helium content down to $3\%$ precision, compared to $5\%$ when using only the brightest star. Finally, the metal-poor binary KIC2971380 hints for a need to correct the $ν_{\rm max}$ scaling relation, supporting recent studies of extremely metal-poor oscillators.

title: Revisiting the Photometric Modulation Amplitudes of Kepler Planet Hosts: A Confounder-Adjusted Test of Stellar Spin-Orbit Alignment
comment: 21 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in AJ
summary: T. Mazeh and coworkers pioneered a method using rotational photometric modulation as a proxy to infer stellar obliquities in Kepler transiting planetary systems, based on the expected positive correlation between spot-induced modulation amplitudes and stellar inclinations. They found that planet hosts cooler than the Sun showed larger modulation amplitudes than comparison stars, consistent with low stellar obliquities. For hotter hosts, however, they reported the opposite - a negative amplitude difference (hosts minus comparison stars) - which is difficult to interpret in terms of viewing geometry. We show that this comparison is affected by confounding variables not controlled for in the sample selection. One such confounder is apparent magnitude, whose distributions differ markedly between the two samples for hotter stars and affect the observed modulation amplitudes. We develop resampling and likelihood-based approaches that enable comparison of the amplitude distributions at fixed apparent magnitude, stellar radius, and rotation period. The previously reported negative amplitude difference for hot hosts is no longer present in either analysis. The likelihood-based analysis finds a positive amplitude difference up to $\sim 6100\,\mathrm{K}$ that becomes consistent with zero at higher temperatures, while the resampling analysis shows a similar but less pronounced trend. This result is qualitatively consistent with independent $v\sin i$ analyses suggesting low obliquities for cooler super-Earth and sub-Neptune hosts and broader obliquity distributions for hotter ones. This may also indicate a gradual change in the obliquity distribution with stellar temperature, although changes in spot distributions or selection effects could also contribute to the photometric trends in hot stars.

title: Detection and characterisation of Starlink VHF TT&C emissions at 137.055 MHz with the 21 CentiMeter Array
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, 4tables. Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Satellite emissions at low frequencies can interfere with astronomical observations. Observations with the EDA2 have revealed recurrent Starlink emissions near 137~MHz, attributed to very high frequency (VHF) telemetry, tracking, and command (TT\&C) transmissions. We aim to characterise Starlink VHF emissions detected with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA) to better assess their potential impact on future low-frequency radio astronomical observations and inform the development of methods to mitigate the resulting interference. We searched five coordinated VHF channels in observations obtained on 15 April 2025 (UTC) and demodulated and decoded candidate signals. Two valid packets are detected at 137.055~MHz, each lasting 1.027584~s and separated by 99.987~s. A blind comparison with 11\,305 active satellites identifies STARLINK-32838 (NORAD ID 62827) as the transmitter, with differential Doppler measurements linking both events to the same spacecraft. Orbital analysis shows that the satellite was undergoing orbit raising and that the limited number of detections was partly attributable to its being below the horizon for most of the observing time. Re-analysis of EDA2 detections indicates that such emissions are not confined to orbit raising. The stronger event's estimated flux density is 9.23~MJy at 1000~km, consistent with previous measurements at the order-of-magnitude level. Signal demodulation and decoding, combined with orbital analysis, can improve the identification and characterisation of satellite-related radio frequency interference. The detection of similar VHF emissions across different orbital phases indicates that their potential interference with low-frequency radio astronomy should not be considered solely in the context of orbit raising.

title: 2:1 Harmonics in the Radio Light Curves of Supermassive Black Hole Binary Candidates
comment: 21 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: We present evidence of 2:1 harmonic periodicities in two supermassive black hole binary (SMBHB) candidates (PKS J0805-0111 and PKS 2131-021) in the Owens Valley Radio Observatory (OVRO) + University of Michigan Radio Astronomical Observatory (UMRAO) monitoring programs. This potential discovery follows the previous detection of a 2:1 harmonic periodicity in the SMBHB candidate J1309+1154 from these programs. If confirmed, these suggest a physical origin of blazars exhibiting strong periodicities favoring 2:1 commensurabilities in their light curves. There are significant differences between the 2:1 harmonics in these three blazars, which may be due to differences in their central engines. These three SMBHB candidates demonstrate the importance of careful dissection, i.e. cutting apart and close examination, of blazar light curves, to reveal underlying evidence of coherence between different aspects of the periodicities observed in blazars in the presence of correlated random noise variations. This is particularly important for blazar SMBHB searches, given that the observed periods thus far are all longer than 2 years, and can disappear for long timespans. Therefore confirming evidence, such as harmonics, may be crucial in confirming the reality of periodicities, and identifying blazar SMBHB candidates. We present four models that can account for 2:1 commensurable periodicities in blazar light curves, together with explanations for why, on these models, shorter period SMBHB candidates have not thus far been observed, but might be anticipated, or not, in the future, depending on the model, thereby making these models discriminatory. Arguments pro and con the reality of these periodicities are presented.

title: Prospects for Near-Far Constraints on Reionization from Simulated LSST Observations of Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies and Stellar Streams
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, submitted to ApJ. Data available at http://app.globus.org/file-manager?origin_id=fef57d95-ed3b-430f-a4a3-132a95d83a00
summary: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will detect resolved stellar populations of intact dwarf galaxies and disrupted stellar streams in the Milky Way (MW) halo and beyond, opening a new avenue for near-field cosmology, particularly for constraining the faint galaxies during reionization. To interpret these data, we present and publicly release mock LSST catalogs of satellites, stellar streams, phase-mixed galaxies, and field galaxies around 13 MW-mass hosts in the FIRE-2 zoom-in simulations, generated with \textsf{py-ananke}. Using a surface brightness limit of $μ_{g} \leq 34$ $\rm{mag}$ $\rm{arcsec^{-2}}$, we find that $\approx29\%$ of streams with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 5 \times 10^5$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable with tidal tails, while another $\approx38\%$ are detectable only through their bound progenitors and would appear as satellites. We estimate that $\approx96\%$ of satellites and $\approx64\%$ of field galaxies (out to $\sim$3.5 Mpc) with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{5}$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable, decreasing to $\approx$59\% and $\approx$42\% for $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{4.5}$ $M_{\odot}$ owing to resolution limits. Including streams detectable as satellites reproduces the radial distribution of observed MW satellites, suggesting that some observed satellites may be bound remnants of disrupted systems. Our mock galaxies match the sizes of observed satellites with $M_{\rm{V}} \lesssim -6$. Star-formation histories computed from only the detectable stars broadly recover the simulated star-formation histories. As an application, we test the near-far technique for reconstructing the proto-MW ultraviolet luminosity function (UVLF) during reionization ($z \gtrsim 6$). Adding the detectable streams improves the recovered faint-end slope at $z = 7$ and reduces the halo-to-halo scatter by $\approx33\%$.

title: All Dark Matter as Primordial Black Holes: a Gravitational-Wave Test
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures
summary: We propose a novel test for the hypothesis that the dark matter of the Universe is composed entirely by asteroidal-mass primordial black holes. It relies on detecting the stochastic gravitational-wave background generated by the coalescence onto rapidly spinning supermassive astrophysical black holes of the light primordial black holes accumulated in spherically symmetric spikes. We discuss the scenarios in which the signal can be observed by the future space-based gravitational-wave observatories LISA and DECIGO.

title: Testing Pre-main-sequence Evolutionary Models with Gaia and SPHEREx Observations of Canis Major North
comment: Accepted for publication in PASP
summary: Pre-main-sequence (PMS) evolutionary models can assign different ages across stellar mass within the same population. We use joint Gaia and SPHEREx spectral energy distributions to infer effective temperatures, radii, and luminosities for members of Canis Major North (CMaN), a nearby association with independent lithium and kinematic age constraints near 23 Myr. The SPHEREx fluxes agree with 2MASS and WISE photometry to 3--6\%, and we anchor the absolute flux scale to Gaia, 2MASS, and WISE. Using the revised temperatures, we obtain a lithium age of $22.4^{+2.8}_{-1.5}$ Myr. For a 29-star PMS sample, population-wide HR-diagram fits yield $20.5^{+1.5}_{-1.4}$ Myr for unspotted SPOTS models, consistent with the external constraints, $18.4^{+1.4}_{-1.3}$ and $18.7^{+1.3}_{-1.2}$ Myr for the Feiden nonmagnetic and BHAC15 models, and substantially older ages of $32.2^{+2.3}_{-2.1}$ and $55^{+5}_{-5}$ Myr for the Feiden magnetic and PARSEC models. No grid returns a temperature-independent age. The Feiden, SPOTS, and BHAC15 models assign older ages to stars above $4000$ K, whereas PARSEC assigns increasingly older ages toward lower temperatures. The intrinsic luminosity dispersion is also mass dependent, approximately $0.14$ dex below $3450$ K but $0.05$ dex at intermediate temperatures. At a fixed age of 23.0 Myr, a single SPOTS filling factor cannot reproduce the width of the low-temperature sequence, whereas the empirical filling-factor distribution of young stars overpredicts it. Spotted isochrones can enclose every cool member only at ages of 37--50 Myr, inconsistent with the lithium and kinematic ages.

title: The impact of the sulfur allotropes and sulfur hydrides on the Venus cloud chemistry
comment: 25 pages, 12 figures, 2 tables
summary: Venus is home to vivid sulfur chemistry, with SO$_2$ as the major sulfur gas species and a global cloud layer between 47 and~70 km composed of H$_2$SO$_4$ and H$_2$O. The chemistry in the clouds has been extensively studied with 1D models, but none is able to reproduce the three orders of magnitude decrease of SO$_2$ inside the clouds. Sulfur allotrope chemistry could be a candidate for buffering sulfur atoms, as it can grow into long chains. Sulfur hydrides such as H$_2$S is considered as one of the main sulfur-bearing compounds, possibly linked to surface reactions or have a volcanic origin like on Earth. In this study, we use for the first time a 3D model to study the climatology of the sulfur allotrope in gas and condensed phase and hydride chemistry in the clouds with an explicit photolysis calculation and updated UV cross-section. H$_2$S is close to ppmv levels below the cloud base, the third most abundant sulfur-bearing species in this region after SO$_2$ and OCS. Below the clouds, S$_8$ gas phase is the most abundant sulfur allotrope. Above, the photolysis and condensation are preponderant, and the gas phase decreases to extremely low values. Polysulfur can therefore not be the unknown absorber at cloud-top altitudes. The condensed phase polysulfurs are present from 30 to above 100~km. S$_2$ condensed phase is the most abundant due to its low saturation mixing ratios. Polysulfur species represent a substantial sulfur reservoir in the upper cloud, equivalent to a few ppmv.

title: A Point-source Catalogue from Direction-dependent Calibrated 21CMA Images
comment: 22 pages, 19 figures, 7 tables. Accepted for publication in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: We present a deep low-frequency radio point-source catalogue centred on the North Celestial Pole (NCP) and extending $5^\circ$ in radius, derived from a single 24-h observation with the 21 CentiMeter Array (21CMA). Covering 75-175 MHz, the catalogue characterises extragalactic foreground point sources for Epoch of Reionization (EoR) studies. Previous 21CMA imaging has been limited by reduced dynamic range caused by direction-dependent effects, particularly the severe grating lobes of ultra-bright sources such as 3C 61.1 and ionospheric phase distortions. Here we apply 21CMAcali, a direction-dependent calibration and imaging pipeline, to mitigate these effects. The angular resolution ranges from 2.3 arcmin at 100 MHz to 1.4 arcmin at 168.75 MHz. The resulting maps show reduced artefacts and background noise, enabling more reliable recovery of faint sources. We construct a catalogue of 1246 radio point sources. Cross-matching with LoTSS-DR3, WENSS, and NVSS enables broad-band spectral fitting, while an independent in-band analysis yields a median spectral index of $α=-0.825$ (where $S \propto ν^α$). The Euclidean-normalised differential source counts at 150 MHz, derived from a dedicated 50-MHz-wide multi-frequency synthesis (MFS) image, are broadly consistent with existing measurements and semi-empirical models at the bright end, whereas the deficit at lower flux densities ($S \lesssim 0.04$ Jy) mainly reflects limited sensitivity and incompleteness. This catalogue improves foreground point-source characterisation in the 21CMA NCP field, demonstrates the value of direction-dependent calibration, and provides a reference for deeper catalogues based on multi-day observations.

title: A microscopic analysis of shear acceleration in the relativistic regime
summary: Relativistic shear flows, as encountered in jets of powerful astrophysical sources, offer promising sites of particle acceleration up to the highest energies. This stochastic acceleration process is usually described with Fokker-Planck transport equations, which assume small momentum gains per scattering. The present paper introduces a covariant microscopic description of relativistic shear acceleration, building on the formalism of generalized Fermi acceleration and formulating angular scattering in the locally comoving frame in terms of stochastic differential equations. This allows us to model relativistic shear profiles and to study the transition from gradual to non-gradual shear acceleration, where the particle mean free path becomes comparable to the shear length scale. Assuming an infinite shear layer, linear in the flow four-velocity, we observe that the shear rate peaks where the flow is mildly relativistic, whereas Lorentz aberration suppresses the transverse velocity of particles where the flow is relativistic. Consequently, particles that leave the central layer experience long waiting times with a heavy-tailed, power-law distribution. The momentum evolution becomes subdiffusive and the acceleration time can substantially exceed local estimates. We successfully reproduce the Monte Carlo energy distributions using a two-state continuous-time random walk with Lévy-distributed waiting times. We also show how a momentum-dependent mean-free path can introduce breaks in the spectrum and extend our discussion to finite jet profiles. These effects should be accounted for in models of relativistic jets as sources of high-energy particles.

title: What sets the star-formation rate in the Milky Way?. II. Comparing the star-forming clumps from simulations and observations
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables, 4 appendices. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary:
Context. Linking the star formation (SF) properties of dense clumps to their parent large-scale environment is a key step to interpret Galactic surveys. Achieving a consistent, multi-scale picture of SF requires a comparative analysis of observations and simulations.
  Aims. We exploit kiloparsec-scale magneto-hydrodynamic simulations designed to reproduce local Milky Way conditions. Leveraging the wide range of scales covered by the simulations (reaching a resolution of 0.03 pc), we aim to compare the properties of the simulated population of star-forming clumps with observational catalogues.
  Methods. After extracting the star-forming structures with the HOP clump-finding algorithm, we compare their physical (mass and size) and SF properties (SF rate and efficiency) with those of the Hi-GAL compact source catalogue.
  Results. Despite the different methodologies and the three-dimensional nature of our clump extraction, the simulated clumps show good agreement with the observed sample in their mass and size distributions. We discover a consistently linear relation between mass and SF rate (SFR) for the simulated clumps, which is remarkably independent of the initial conditions of the boxes. Using scaling relations to distinguish between turbulence- and gravity-regulated gas inflow onto the clump scales, we find tentative evidence in favour of a gravity-regulated regime of SF at the probed sub-parsec scales.
  Key words. methods: numerical - stars: formation - ISM: clouds

title: Non-minimal $α$-attractor magnetogenesis with potential dependent couplings
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables
summary: We investigate inflationary magnetogenesis driven by a non conformal coupling in the case of large-field $α$-attractor inspired models. We introduce potential-dependent electromagnetic coupling functions $f(φ)$ that reproduce the scaling $f\propto a^p$ during slow roll. Starting from Starobinsky inflation, we analytically derive explicit couplings for $(E)$-model and $(T)$-model potentials. We then study how these functions affect electromagnetic amplification in the regime of non-minimal coupling between the inflaton field and the Ricci scalar $φ^2 R$. In particular, we compare different values for the coupling strength $ξ$, accounting for electromagnetic backreaction and Schwinger pair production through the gradient expansion formalism. Our numerical results show that the non-minimal coupling affects the evolution of the electromagnetic sector and the resulting magnetic-field amplitude. We find that, within the analyzed configurations, minimally coupled and $ξ>0$ scenarios are compatible with the adopted CMB constraints, yielding conditional present-day magnetic-field estimates of order $10^{-23}$ G.

title: Dynamical plausibility of triple-assisted interaction in Be-star multiple systems
summary: Classical Be stars are rapidly rotating B-type stars surrounded by gaseous circumstellar disks, but the origin of their angular momentum remains uncertain. We investigate whether observed Be-star multiple systems are dynamically compatible with triple-assisted interaction, in which a tertiary companion drives Kozai-Lidov (KL) eccentricity excitation in an unresolved inner binary. We combine speckle-interferometric detections, reported inner periods, and proper-motion anomalies (PMa) with synthetic populations of hierarchical triples. Accepted configurations must satisfy dynamical stability, secular-timescale, inner-periastron interaction, and observational constraints. Refined mass-aware simulations identify HD 35079 and HD 55606 as the clearest period-plus-speckle dynamical matches. HD 205329 remains dynamically plausible but depends on the approximate PMa constraint. For HD 41335, the period-plus-speckle and PMa-plus-speckle constraints are separately compatible, whereas imposing all three simultaneously yields no accepted configurations at the adopted tolerance. HD 37330, HD 41600, and HD 71510 are additional PMa-dependent hierarchical-triple candidates. An independent angular-momentum estimate indicates a median required accreted mass fraction of approximately 4.8% under the adopted assumptions. We conclude that several observed Be-star multiple systems admit stable, KL-active architectures capable of driving inner binaries toward interaction. These results establish dynamical plausibility rather than a confirmed evolutionary history and motivate further speckle, spectroscopic, and astrometric monitoring.

title: Unbound grains in gaseous debris discs
summary: Context. Some debris discs contain cold molecular gas. The origin of this gas is one of the key questions in our understanding of the evolution of planetary systems. The effect of gas on the smallest dust grains, which are expected to be unbound due to radiation pressure, is not well understood. The unbound grains contribute to the brightness of scattered light and thermal emission from the disc halo at short wavelengths. Aims. We explored the conditions under which gas can prevent or slow down the escape of unbound grains and increase their number density in the disc halo sufficiently to affect its brightness and reveal properties of the gas. Methods. We numerically integrated the equations of motion of dust grains released on unbound orbits in optically thin, gaseous debris discs, taking into account stellar gravity, radiation pressure, Poynting-Robertson drag, and gas drag. Results. We find that gas drag can significantly slow down the escape of unbound grains only for very high gas masses, such as those expected if the gas is remnant protoplanetary gas and not of secondary origin. We also present an analytical model for estimating the density of unbound grains in gaseous discs. Conclusions. If a difference in the abundance of unbound grains between gaseous and non-gaseous debris discs were observed, it would imply that the gas in debris discs is protoplanetary. Currently, there is no evidence of such a difference, suggesting that the gas detected in debris discs is either secondary or strongly depleted protoplanetary gas.

title: A Fast and Memory-Efficient Algorithm for Searching Faint Moving Objects using Synthetic Tracking
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures
summary: Detecting unknown faint moving objects using optical imaging is challenging. Long exposure times are infeasible for such targets, as the resulting image streaking causes a loss of signal-to-noise ratio due to energy dispersal across multiple pixels. To address this, synthetic tracking, a track-before-detect method, replaces long exposures with many short exposures, integrating them in post-processing to recover the moving signal. Enabled by modern CMOS detectors with fast readout and low read noise, this technique synthesizes telescope tracking by searching over a grid of velocities. However, the conventional brute-force implementation imposes a significant computational burden: integrating N_f frames of size (N_x,N_y) requires O(N_x N_y N_f^3) operations. This cost becomes prohibitive for megapixel-scale frames with N_f~100. Although dynamic programming can reduce the computational complexity by a factor of N_f, it requires a prohibitive memory of O(N_x N_y N_f^2), unsuitable for large-format detectors. This article presents a novel algorithm to achieve the computational efficiency of dynamic programming while maintaining a memory footprint of just O(N_x N_y N_f) by slightly approximating the computation of frame shifts for alignment. By expressing the shift as a sum of terms proportional to the digits frame index in binary and rounding up each of these terms, frames can be integrated efficiently by hierarchically adding intermediate sums that are shared across different velocities with the same higher bits in binary. The approximation only introduces a small tracking error that increases logarithmically with the number of frames. This advancement enables synthetic tracking to be executed with high energy efficiency, making it practical for deployment on standard workstations rather than requiring high-performance computing infrastructure such as GPU servers or CPU clusters.

title: History of Turn-Ons - the irregular 35-day clock - of Hercules X-1
comment: 21 pages, 15 figures
summary: Hercules X-1 and Centaurus X-3 are the first ever detected - and as such identified - binary X-ray pulsars. Here we concern ourselves with the 35-day flux modulation of Her X-1, immediately found at its discovery, together with the binary period of 1.7 days and the pulsation with 1.24 s. The 35-day flux modulation shows two flux maxima, the so-called Main-On and the Short-On (with reduced flux). As noticed early on, the period, or the length of the cycle, is variable. The system constitutes an irregular clock, with a more or less stable mean period of near 34.85 d. We consider the repeated rapid increases of the flux from the off-state to the Main-On (the socalled Turn-Ons) as the best timing marker to study this clock. Here we present a complete list of Turn-On times over 55 years, from the discovery of Her X-1 to today (2026), based on historic work from the literature and on observational data provided by five monitoring instruments. We identify to following basic features of the irregular 35-day clock: The Turn-Ons show preference to occur at orbital phases 0.25 and 0.75. The duration of the 35-day cycle clusters around three discrete values - 20.0, 20.5 and 21.0 orbital cycles with a dominant peak at 20.5 Porb (57%). The long-term trend in the 35-day period duration is seen in the O-C (Observed minus Calculated) diagram. There are two sections, separated by the long Anomalous Low of 1999/200 (AL3), which can be modeled by parabolic functions with a smooth evolution of the 35-day period. A medium-term variation is observed in the form of Anomalous Lows, an essential shut-off (at least of soft) X-rays. We find an apparent underlying period of 5.4 yr. There are short-term (hundreds of days) variations (in part quasi-periodic) overlaid to the long-term trend. Straight ups and downs in the O-C diagram, demonstrating rather rapid 35 day period changes.

title: The Cosmic Ultraviolet Baryon Survey X: Density and Pressure Profiles of Clumpy Circumgalactic Gas at $z=0.4-0.7$
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal after minor revisions. 24 pages with 8 figures, and a 27-page appendix with 23 additional figures
summary: The thermodynamic state and turbulent properties of the cool circumgalactic medium (CGM) are investigated for 23 galaxies and galaxy groups at intermediate redshift ($z=0.4$--0.7) in the Cosmic Ultraviolet Baryon Survey (CUBS) midz sample using background QSOs within the virial radius. Kinematically resolved absorption-line measurements from Hubble Space Telescope/COS and STIS spectra, combined with photoionization modeling, yield gas densities of $n_\mathrm{H}\approx10^{-4}$--$10^{-2} \ \mathrm{cm}^{-3}$, temperatures of $T\approx(1$--$5) \times 10^4\,\mathrm{K}$, and non-thermal line broadening of $b_\mathrm{NT}\approx2$--$30 \ \mathrm{km \ s^{-1}}$ for individual cool clumps. Combined with published samples at similar redshifts, the results indicate that photoionization equilibrium accurately describes the cool CGM and that turbulent motions are predominantly subsonic. At fixed projected distance, cool-gas density decreases systematically with halo mass, while inferred cool-gas pressures in $M_h\approx10^{12}$--$10^{13}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ halos are consistent with hot-gas pressures inferred from stacked X-ray observations. The analysis uncovers a near constant total cool gas mass across a broad halo mass range, which directly translates to a declining baryon mass fraction in the cool phase from $\approx 6$--$19\%$ in halos of $M_h \approx 10^{12}\, \mathrm{M}_\odot$ to $\approx 0.6$--$1.5\%$ in halos of $M_h \approx 10^{13}\, \mathrm{M}_\odot$. Finally, several CUBS galaxies exhibit kinematically aligned low- and high-ionization species spanning up to two orders of magnitude in density, reflecting local fluctuations in the halo gas pressure.

title: Towards Reliably Measuring the Mass-Size Relation of Dark Matter Halos: Impact of projection, miscentering and Eddington bias
comment: 25 pages, 18 figures. Comments and feedback welcome
summary: In the conventional spherical overdensity definition of a dark matter halo, masses and radii, e.g. $M_{200{\rm m}}$ and $r_{200{\rm m}}$, are equivalent. However, halos do exhibit a physical boundary at the splashback radius $r_{\rm sp}$, which manifests as a sharp drop in density. Splashback radii are now routinely measured in stacked weak lensing profiles, but the expected trend of decreasing $r_{\rm sp}/r_{200{\rm m}}$ with mass has not been verified in observed galaxy groups or clusters. In this work, we show that several observational effects conceal the predicted mass-size relation. In particular, we quantify the impact of systematics on the mean density and lensing profiles of mock-observed halo samples, which are created by applying a realistic cluster-finding procedure to dark matter-only simulations. We reproduce the known impact of projection: preferentially observing systems in overdense regions. But, differing from previous works, we show that the same projection effect, combined with scatter in observed luminosities, causes a significant Eddington bias in the derived mass-observable relation and a complex suppression in mean density profiles over all radial scales. The magnitude of this effect is mass-dependent and coupled to the cluster-finding procedure and survey properties, making it challenging to model simply and motivating full forward-modeling of observed group and cluster samples. However, we demonstrate that a simple mitigation approach, effectively a weak lensing mass calibration, does well in approximately recovering the true mass-size relation. Finally, we show that only severe miscentering can bias the measurement of the halo size, but any miscentering can increase the measurement uncertainty.

title: Calculation of distant retrograde orbits and their use in space weather forecasting
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: There is current renewed interest in using Sun-Earth distant retrograde orbits (DROs) for a space weather forecasting mission, which would temporarily place spacecraft at a position near the Sun-Earth line, but closer to the Sun than the L1 point (such as the ESA HENON mission and ESA SHIELD concept). With in situ observations of the magnetic field on a DRO, the southward ($B_z < 0$) magnetic field of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs), which is not routinely accessible remotely, could be measured several hours in advance. This $B_z < 0$ field is a decisive factor for forecasting geomagnetic storm intensity. We present an analysis of DROs at different sub-L1 distances for their efficacy for a space weather forecasting mission. An open-source numerical framework to generate DRO trajectories is presented. Our pre-calculated orbits in Heliocentric Earth Ecliptic coordinates can be introduced into numerical or empirical simulations of the ambient solar wind and ICMEs. We then analyze the corresponding forecast lead times, the resulting observational gaps depending on the number of spacecraft and distance of a DRO, and the "cone of acceptance" of the maximum longitudinal separation of a spacecraft to the Sun-Earth line. We define different domains regarding radial evolution and longitudinal CME structure, and show the historical coverage of sub-L1 ICME observations with our ICMECAT catalog. An optimal mission configuration can be selected based on the characteristics of DROs presented here, depending on the requirements of such a mission deemed acceptable with respect to results on CME evolution and coherence.

title: JWST/MIRI Observations of Amorphous Silicates in Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
comment: submitted to ApJL
summary: We present JWST/MIRI Low Resolution Spectroscopy (LRS) of 3I/ATLAS obtained post-perihelion at a heliocentric distance of 2.21 au. Our spectrum contains a prominent 10 micron silicate emission feature with a broad, smooth shape that is distinct from those commonly observed in Solar System comets. We model the spectrum using thermal emission from amorphous carbon, amorphous olivine, and amorphous pyroxene grains. Our models strongly favor a pyroxene-dominated, amorphous silicate composition and show a degeneracy between silicate grain size and the relative abundance of silicate and carbon dust. Across a set of representative models, the best-fitting crystalline abundance is zero, and we place an upper limit of 5.3% on the crystalline fraction of the silicates. We identify an emission feature near 6.83 microns that is consistent with aliphatic C-H-bearing material. The overwhelmingly amorphous silicate composition supports previous work that measured unusual volatile and isotopic composition in suggesting that the material incorporated into the object experienced little thermal processing and preserves information about the conditions in which this interstellar planetesimal formed.

title: ECH0EZ: Estimating the Hubble constant with ZTF SN Ia DR2
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures (+ appendix)
summary: Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are instrumental for a precise measurement of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) from the local distance ladder, yet the data used hitherto for this purpose are inhomogeneous and subject to severe selection effects. We present the first, preliminary, cosmological analysis of 772 SNe Ia from the Zwicky Transient Facility's second data release: an untargeted single-telescope sample whose volume-limited subset (z<0.06) is largely free of Malmquist bias. We correct the public data for known instrumental and calibration biases and the redshifts for peculiar motions. Using the 42 SH0ES calibrators (their host distances computed from Cepheids and geometric anchors) and a Bayesian hierarchical model of SN Ia standardisation, dust extinction, redshift and calibration uncertainties, we infer $H_0 = (71.6 \pm 1.5)$ km/s/Mpc after marginalising over deceleration with a flat prior (or $(72.3 \pm 1.1)$ km/s/Mpc if a prior on matter density from Pantheon+ is imposed), with the uncertainty dominated by the number of calibrators.
