title: Discovery of a New Electron Spectrum Produced by Fast Cooling of Relativistic Electrons
comment: accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: In energetic astrophysical sources like the gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) and blazars, the relativistic electrons lose their energy efficiently through synchrotron radiation and inverse Compton (IC) scattering and can rapidly cool to energies below the minimum acceleration energy $γ_m$. It is widely known that such electrons develop a power-law spectrum $γ_e^{-2}$ below $γ_m$. However, this power-law spectrum is valid only if a steady-state population of electrons is assumed. In general, the cooled electrons below $γ_m$ evolve in a non-steady state and their spectrum deviates significantly from the power-law $γ_e^{-2}$. We present here a new electron spectrum $f_{\rm U}$ that describes this fast-cooled, generally-evolving, and non-steady-state population of electrons below $γ_m$. We consider two cooling cases: (1) when the electrons undergo radiative (i.e., synchrotron + IC) cooling, and (2) when the electrons experience both radiative and adiabatic cooling. We first derive $f_{\rm U}$ analytically and find an explicit expression of $f_{\rm U}$ for each cooling case. Secondly, we show that $f_{\rm U}$ is a solution to a Fokker-Planck equation in the entire energy range below $γ_m$ and derive a general version of $f_{\rm U}$ for each cooling case. We also compare $f_{\rm U}$ to a detailed numerical calculation of a blazar electron spectrum and find an excellent agreement for the whole energy range below $γ_m$. Thus, $f_{\rm U}$ gives us a general electron spectrum to describe the entire cooled electrons below $γ_m$. Our discovery of a new fast-cooling solution $f_{\rm U}$ below $γ_m$ may find it applicable in a wide range of energetic phenomena in high-energy astrophysics.

title: Heavy Seeds and the Multi-scale Fueling of Early Supermassive Black Holes and Little Red Dots
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to ApJ

Cosmological simulations investigating their formation and evolution confront the limitation that the compact scale of SMBH/LRD physics cannot be simultaneously resolved with the larger-scale cosmological environment. We address this limitation by utilizing a cutout technique, selecting a targeted region around an SMBH seed from a cosmological parent simulation and re-running the cutout at higher (sub-pc) resolution for shorter periods. We explore two SMBH formation scenarios: the standard, light seed stellar-remnant case, and the heavy-seed, direct collapse black hole (DCBH) channel. Within the high-resolution achieved by the cutouts, the DCBH, due to its larger mass, is able to induce a buildup of high density gas nearby and accrete gas in bursts of super-Eddington phases, growing in mass and producing an LRD-like spectrum. In contrast, the stellar remnant cannot do so and remains dormant, unable to affect the nearby gas or significantly evolve by gas accretion alone. Therefore, we find that observed high-redshift SMBHs and LRDs require the existence of heavy seeds to assemble dense gas around themselves, enabling efficient growth and producing red optical spectra with strong Balmer breaks resembling LRDs.

title: Warm inflation beyond the Gaussian limit: primordial black holes and induced gravitational waves
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures
summary: In warm inflation, the primordial fluctuations are driven by random kicks from a hot radiation bath. Two features of these kicks matter: how long the bath remembers them, which shapes the power spectrum, and how their strengths are spread, which controls the rare, extreme fluctuations. In this paper, we investigate how primordial black holes and the accompanying induced gravitational waves can be used to discriminate between these two features. We use a simple model inspired by warm inflation, in which independent kicks of random strength add up to a narrow peak in the power spectrum. At leading order, the induced gravitational wave depends only on the power spectrum and is therefore insensitive to how the kicks are distributed. However, the black holes are very sensitive to these rare large fluctuations. Hence, two baths can yield the same gravitational wave signal while forming black holes at very different rates. A modest kurtosis range of 0.1 to 0.3 enhances black-hole formation by factors of ten to a million at fixed gravitational-wave amplitude, the larger factors for the rarer black holes. Counting peaks rather than all points, or widening the spectrum, lowers the enhancement by at most a factor of about four. In general a change in the power affects both phenomena, while the kurtosis affects only the black hole production.

title: Periodic radio emission from a rapidly rotating T8 ultracool dwarf
comment: Accepted for publication in PASA
summary: We report the discovery of periodic radio bursts from the T8 brown dwarf WISE J151721.13+052929.3 (WISE J1517+05), detected with ASKAP and MeerKAT. title: Propulsion Systems for a Starshade Rendezvous Mission with the Habitable World Observatory
comment: 39 pages, 11 figure, 4 tables. Accepted for publication on JATIS

title: CROMA: a GPU-accelerated Fokker--Planck solver for modeling non-thermal emission in post-processing cosmological simulations
comment: 15 pages, submitted to Astronomy & Computing

An increasing number of studies employ FP solvers coupled with magnetohydrodynamical (MHD) simulations to follow the evolution of CRs in dynamically evolving environments. We present a new C/C++-based FP solver with GPU acceleration for post-processing outputs from cosmological MHD simulations. The code evolves CR proton and electron spectra along Lagrangian tracer trajectories and consistently includes re-acceleration and secondary-particle production processes. With the Chang--Cooper finite-difference scheme, the FP equation for each tracer is reduced to an independent tridiagonal system, which is solved on NVIDIA GPUs using a CUDA implementation of the parallel cyclic reduction (PCR) algorithm. The code uses sub-stepping between tracer snapshots, with the timestep constrained by the relevant CR cooling or re-acceleration timescale, and a batching algorithm that groups tracers with similar sub-stepping patterns for efficient execution. We find that the GPU acceleration increases the per-node throughput by a factor of $\approx$10 on the Leonardo Booster system operated by CINECA. The fast FP solver is useful for high-resolution simulations dedicated to comparison with next-generation radio observations and future multi-messenger applications combining radio, gamma-ray, and high-energy neutrino observations.

title: Self lensing in BH-NS binaries as progenitors for periodically repeating Fast Radio Bursts
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are bright extragalactic transients whose origin remains uncertain. The discovery of repeating FRBs, some with cyclic activity windows, opens new prospects for testing their progenitors. Neutron stars (NSs) are strong candidates, as they naturally emit radio pulses with temporal and spectral properties resembling those of FRBs, an interpretation reinforced by the detection of an FRB-like burst from the Galactic magnetar SGR 1935+2154. Nevertheless, the pulse energy of typical radio-emitting NSs remains several orders of magnitude below that of even the faintest observed FRBs. We explore a binary system in which a NS orbits a black hole (BH), so that NS radio pulses are gravitationally amplified through self-lensing, producing characteristic signatures in the energy distribution, activity windows, and waiting times that can be contrasted with observations. We implement a simple NS-BH binary model with a circular orbit undergoing Lense-Thirring precession, and compute how the pulses are lensed along the orbit, including pulse splitting and time delays. Pure Keplerian orbits produce activity windows several orders of magnitude shorter than those of periodic FRBs. Post-Keplerian orbits with Lense-Thirring precession are more promising, yielding windows of a few to tens of days. Lensing transforms an intrinsic log-normal NS pulse-energy distribution, producing a high-energy power-law tail spanning up to four orders of magnitude. Interpreting the observed millisecond waiting times between consecutive bursts as lensing-induced image delays, we infer BH masses of 10^3-10^4 solar masses, in the intermediate-mass (IMBH) range. However, the amplification in our model is insufficient to bridge the energy gap between Galactic magnetar radio pulses and FRBs. Moreover, the non-detection of NS-IMBH systems suggests a low abundance, so this channel is likely rare.

title: Protostellar Outflows at the EarliesT Stages (POETS) X. Preliminary statistics of 6.7 GHz masers near POETS sources
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures
summary: So far, the POETS survey has focused on studying at high angular resolution the properties of both 22.2 GHz H2O masers and the radio continuum emission near young stellar objects (YSOs). We seek to probe the existence of 6.7 GHz maser emission near POETS sources with high sensitivity observations and study their kinematic properties with respect to local radio continuum and 22.2 GHz maser emission at high angular and spectral resolutions. Within the POETS survey, we used the Very Large Array (VLA) in the A configuration, operating at high spectral resolution (0.1 km/s) and achieving a sensitivity of a few mJy/beam per channel map, in order to (i) probe the emission from methanol gas in the 6.7 GHz maser transition and (ii) trace its absolute spatial distribution and local standard of rest velocity. We present a preliminary analysis of 6.7 GHz CH3OH maser emission toward a subsample of the POETS survey (22 fields observed so far), 60 % of which show detection above a brightness temperature threshold of 10^7 K. Five sources among this subsample are new detections. We draw a 6.7 GHz maser brightness function by studying the distribution of the intrinsic luminosity of the maser population and predict that more than 30 % of the whole population is undetected at typical interferometric sensitivities of a few 10 mJy/beam. We confirm that 6.7 GHz masers arise close to the young star they are associated with and quantify that, on average, 90 % of them are distributed within radii of 3000 au only. Furthermore, we find a tight correlation between the 6.7 GHz maser luminosity coming from a given source and the local free-free emission, suggesting that the radio continuum provides the dominant source of seed photons amplified by the methanol gas.

title: Relativistic N-body simulations with mass-varying neutrinos
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures
summary: Recent cosmological data provide weak hints for smaller masses than what is required by neutrino-oscillation experiments, motivating investigations into variation of the neutrino masses with cosmic time. Here we study a model where the neutrinos couple to a quintessence field that acts as dark energy. We compute structure formation using fully dynamical and relativistic N-body and lattice simulations, with nonlinear field evolution and a weak-field metric expansion. Similar to previous studies, we find the generic appearance of neutrino lumps, but observe them to be highly dynamical and spinning. We study several models where the effective dark energy, including nonlinear effects of the scalar field on the cosmic expansion, can show phantom crossing. The relativistic physics available in our simulation framework can help distinguish such models from LCDM, through observations of neutrino and dark energy properties, and slip between the gravitational potentials due to anisotropic stress. The rich phenomenology offered by mass-varying neutrinos motivates further exploration and development of the simulation techniques.

title: Heating of Solar Coronal Loops by Converging Unipolar Magnetic Flux: Evidence from SDO Observations and a Radiative MHD Simulation
comment: 28 pages, 17 figures; to appear in ApJ
summary: Solar coronal loop heating remains one of the greatest mysteries in astrophysics. This behavior is similar to recent findings for solar coronal plumes. To investigate and quantify this effect, we track 10 QR coronal loops through their lifetimes using SDO/AIA 171 and 94 Angstrom images, along with SDO/HMI magnetograms. The coronal EUV luminosity shows a strong correlation with the magnetic flux in at least one footpoint, most strongly when the line-of-sight magnetic field strength (Blos) exceeds a threshold of about 200-500 G. A Bifrost MHD simulation of the quiet-Sun network and corona shows similar behavior but at smaller time-scales: magnetic flux convergence and divergence -- most pronounced at a loop footpoint -- correlate directly with increased and reduced emissivity due to heating and cooling, respectively. The simulation reveals an increase in Poynting flux, reconnection, and Joule heating with flux convergence at that footpoint. We hypothesize that an increased rate of nanoflares during flux convergence may explain the enhanced emissivity of these loops due to heating, with potentially broader implications for coronal heating.

authors: for the PLATO Stellar Variability Working Group
title: Measuring masses of transiting Earth-like planets: first insights from the PLATO RV data challenge
summary:
The PLATO Stellar Variability Mitigation Working Group designed a radial-velocity (RV) data challenge to assess the precision and accuracy achievable on RV semi-amplitudes in the context of the future PLATO follow-up.
  Using Sun-as-a-star observations obtained with HARPS-N, we generated three multi-planet systems with realistic sampling, an effective signal-to-noise ratio of S/N ~ 450, an exposure time of 15 minutes, and a total of approximately 1000 observations. The resulting data set is publicly available and can serve as a benchmark for the community to test and compare RV analysis methods. Eight independent teams participated in the challenge, aiming to recover the semi-amplitudes of both transiting and non-transiting planets.
  A meta-analysis of the submitted results shows that, with current data analysis methods, HARPS-N-like stability and the observing strategy studied in this paper, achieving a precision on semi-amplitudes better than 10% for habitable-zone signals around a solar-type star is challenging, and is typically limited to planets with masses of approximately 8-10 Earth masses. This performance is expected to improve for K dwarfs, where planets down to approximately 2-5 Earth masses may be characterized at a similar level of precision.
  Finally, based on the results of this challenge and the occurrence of false positives, we derive an empirical detection threshold for RV surveys, which can be used to distinguish robust planetary detections from candidates.

title: X-ray Emission Study of TeV Blazars
comment: 21 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJS
summary: In this work, we present a systematic X-ray study of 85 TeV-detected blazars based on archival \emph{Swift}-XRT and \emph{NuSTAR} observations available up to May 2024. We derive unabsorbed X-ray fluxes and photon indices through spectral fitting, and investigate their light curves, spectral energy distributions, flux distributions, power spectral densities, and flux-index correlations. Using the fractional variability method, we identify 78 sources as variable in the soft X-ray band and 14 sources as variable in the hard X-ray band. For well-sampled soft X-ray light curves, the flux distributions are generally better described by log-normal functions, while the PSD slopes span $β_{\rm PSD}=0.1$--$1.6$, with most values between 1.0 and 1.6, where the PSD is defined as $P(f)\propto f^{-β_{\rm PSD}}$. We find positive correlations between TeV and X-ray luminosities, supporting a leptonic emission scenario. We also find a correlation between X-ray and disk luminosities, whereas no significant correlation is found between X-ray luminosity and black hole mass.

title: The inner galaxy as a window on its early assembly: lessons from a cosmological Milky Way analogue
comment: 19 pages, 14 figures, 1 table, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Characterising the assembly history of the inner Milky Way is a key goal of upcoming spectroscopic surveys, yet disentangling its overlapping stellar components remains challenging. We investigate the chemodynamics of the centre of a Milky Way analogue in the Auriga Superstars cosmological hydrodynamical simulation suite, focusing on a high-resolution halo (~ 800 M_sun star particles) with a realistic galactic bar and accretion history. We classify stars within the inner 4 kpc into proto-galaxy, subsequent in-situ, and accreted components to assess their distinguishability using kinematics, dynamics, ages, and metallicities. Stellar net rotation declines sharply between [Fe/H]=0 and [Fe/H]=-1, marking the transition from disc-like in-situ stars to the proto-galaxy. While significant chemical and dynamical overlaps complicate the search for structures in energy-angular momentum (E-Lz) space, metal-poor stars ([Fe/H]<-1) at low energy form a remarkably pure (>97%) sample of proto-galaxy stars. Conversely, the high-energy, metal-poor tail offers the best chance of detecting accreted debris. However, at high energies the inner accreted halo is dominated by low-mass systems (M_star ~ 10^7 - 10^9 M _sun), not the earliest massive mergers. Dynamically, few clues remain from early mergers, and early enrichment is rapid and similar across progenitors. In-situ contamination is an issue for [Fe/H]>-1 throughout E-Lz space. Overall, while accurate stellar ages and high-precision chemical abundances may help further constrain the Milky Way's history, we should be cautious when associating stars with individual merger events in the inner galaxy.

title: Cosmological constraints on single-field inflation models from ACT/SPT data and observations at sub-Mpc scales
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures
summary: We investigate single-field inflation models that can produce large curvature perturbations at sub-Mpc scales while remaining consistent with cosmological observations across multiple regimes. We highlight the tension between generating enhanced small-scale perturbations and maintaining agreement with the scalar spectral index $n_s$ measured by ACT and SPT, which disfavors several conventional single-field inflation models. To address this issue, we propose three viable classes of inflationary potentials: bump/dip-modified, step-like, and double-inflection-point. Each can sufficiently amplify primordial perturbations while predicting $n_s$ that lie within the $2σ$ range of current observational bounds. In addition, we examine the primordial power spectra predicted by these models and constrain their parameter spaces using cosmological observations at different scales, including CMB, BAO, PBH, PTA, and CMB-distortion. Our results show that some of the models considered can simultaneously satisfy the ACT/SPT constraints and account for the current PTA observations, although doing so while respecting the constraints on the PBH abundance remains challenging.

title: The formation of silicon-carbon chain molecules in IRC+10216
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS, 9 pages including one appendix
summary: Linear silicon-carbon chain molecules, SiC$_n$ (n = 3--6), have been detected in the circumstellar envelope of the carbon-rich AGB star IRC+10216. Using a combination of measured and postulated rate coefficients, we show that the column densities of the silicon carbide molecules observed in IRC+10216 can be reproduced to with a factor of four. Furthermore, our model calculations suggest that the column densities of SiC$_7$ and SiC$_8$ are a factor of 2--4 less than that of SiC$_6$. We discuss the influence of neutral-neutral reactions involving parent SiC$_2$ on chain growth and show that their neglect leads to a reduction in column densities of carbides up to a maximum of about six for SiC$_6$ and SiC$_7$. Our results suggest that the detection of SiC$_7$ and SiC$_8$ in IRC+10216 will be challenging but that astronomical searches should be undertaken.

Notably, we also observe a polarisation reversal within a single burst profile, which is currently unexplained. We model the emission using a dipolar magnetic field with emission arising from a single active field line, and find a moderate inclination angle of $i = 47.9^{+11.4}_{-9.2}$ degrees and a magnetic obliquity of $β= 40.1^{+9.2}_{-10.9}$ degrees. WISE J1517+05 expands the parameter space of radio-active UCDs toward higher luminosities and lower polarisation fractions, suggesting that current surveys may be sensitive to a larger population than previously recognised, while searches relying on methods that assume high circular polarisation fractions risk missing a subset of UCDs. More broadly, this discovery reinforces the idea that rapid rotation plays a key role in generating strong dipolar magnetic fields in UCDs that can give rise to auroral radio emission.

title: Reconstruction of very inclined air showers with radio data and application to the first GRANDProto300 cosmic-ray candidates
comment: Presented at the 60th Rencontres de Moriond on Very High Energy Phenomena in the Universe (Moriond VHEPU 2026). 4 pages, 5 figures
summary: Radio detection of very inclined extensive air showers (EAS) offers a promising way to study ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) and neutrinos above $10^{17}$ eV. We present a method to reconstruct the arrival direction and energy of EAS with zenith angles above $60^\circ$, applicable in principle to upward-going neutrino-induced showers. The approach combines a point-source-like description of the radio wavefront with the Angular Distribution Function (ADF), a phenomenological model describing the angular pattern of electric field amplitudes in the 50-200 MHz band. On realistic cosmic-ray simulations, we achieve better than $0.07^\circ$ resolution on arrival direction and ~15\% on primary energy. Applied directly to voltage traces, this method allows efficient cosmic-ray selection with accurate direction reconstruction and first-order energy estimation. We illustrate the method on the first cosmic-ray candidates detected by the GRANDProto300 prototype of GRAND, validating its detection principle and paving the way for high-precision neutrino searches.

title: Coherent Radio Emission from Flux Rope Mergers in 3D Relativistic Reconnection
comment: 13 pages, submitted to ApJ
summary: Coherent emission from merging plasmoids in relativistic reconnection is the leading model for radio emission originating in the outer magnetosphere of pulsars such as the Crab, and a candidate emission mechanism for fast radio bursts. This process has only been studied in 2D, and whether it survives in 3D, where the dynamics of structures in the reconnection layer can differ substantially, is still an open question. Here we present the first study of coherent wave generation from flux rope mergers in 3D relativistic reconnection. We use particle-in-cell simulations of relativistic reconnection with outflow boundary conditions and guide fields $B_g/B_0 = \{0,0.1,0.3\}$, and measure the efficiency $η$ with which inflowing magnetic energy is converted into escaping coherent waves. We find $η\sim 7\times10^{-4}$ without a guide field, a factor of a few below 2D results, and $η\sim(1\text{-}2) \times10^{-3}$ at moderate guide fields, comparable to 2D with no guide field. We propose a physical picture for why the efficiency remains comparable to 2D, based on how reconnected field is transported away from the diffusion regions. The escaping waves are linearly polarized, with a polarization angle set by the direction of the upstream field. In the presence of a guide field, waves escaping from opposite sides of the reconnection layer therefore differ in polarization angle by $ \sim 2\arctan(B_g/B_0)$. Our results support relativistic magnetic reconnection as the origin of coherent radio emission from Crab-like pulsars, and strengthen its case as a potential emission mechanism for fast radio bursts.

title: Unveiling the nonthermal environments of NGC 3411 and NGC 5903 through new MeerKAT observations
summary: Galaxy groups are key laboratories for investigating the interplay between active galactic nucleus (AGN) outbursts and the dynamical processes of the intra-group medium. We aim to characterize the morphology, spectral properties, and magnetic field structure of the diffuse nonthermal radio emission in two peculiar galaxy groups, NGC 3411 and NGC 5903, selected from an originally larger sample, in order to constrain its origin and its connection with the dynamics of the intra-group medium. We present new MeerKAT UHF- and L-band observations of the two groups, complemented by archival Chandra and XMM-Newton data already analyzed in previous works. In NGC 3411, we detect extended radio emission surrounding the central AGN over scales of ~70 kpc, and resolve previously undetected arc-shaped substructures on scales of ~20-30 kpc. This extended component exhibits a relatively uniform steep spectrum ($α$ ~ -1.7). We discuss possible scenarios for its origin, including mini-halos, aged AGN plasma, weak shocks, and the possibility of a radio galaxy observed along the line of sight. In NGC 5903, MeerKAT reveals a complex filamentary morphology, including a previously unknown ring-like structure surrounding the central AGN. Spectral-index mapping shows localized flattening ($α$ ~ -0.9) along the north arc, while polarization data reveal ordered magnetic fields and a patchy rotation measure distribution across the source. Together with the disturbed X-ray morphology, these results support a scenario in which fossil AGN plasma has been redistributed and locally reenergized by group-scale dynamical processes such as turbulence, shear, and weak compression. Our results demonstrate that galaxy groups can host a rich variety of nonthermal phenomena, whose properties can only be fully revealed through the combination of sensitive, high-resolution, and multifrequency radio observations.

title: Getting Ready For Analysing Rubin Data : CLMM v2, The Updated LSST-DESC Cluster Weak Lensing Mass Modeling Library For Cosmology
comment: 10 pages, 12 figures
summary: The Dark Energy Science Collaboration has prepared a multitude of pipelines to process the upcoming Vera C. Rubin Observatory data and perform different scientific analyses. Here, we present the methodology to constrain the mass information of galaxy clusters from weak lensing, which is encompassed by the v2.0 release of the Cluster Lensing Mass Modeling (CLMM) code. This Python library provides the ingredients for both the modeling and data reduction of lensing observables, and the improvements in the new version were customized to handle the first WL analyses of LSST clusters, including, e.g., stacking functionalities and WL multipoles. This new version of CLMM has allowed various cluster analyses using LSST-DESC simulated data, precursor survey and Rubin commissioning and survey validation data, and is ready to be used for the first cluster cosmology analyses. CLMM is an open-source software package collaboratively written in Python, providing multiple example notebooks, including a set that can reproduce all figures in this work, and extensive documentation, publicly available at https://lsstdesc.org/CLMM/.

title: Three-dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Shocks and Associated Plasma Heating in the Solar Atmosphere
comment: Accepted for publication in ApJ. 17 pages, 9 figures
summary: We investigate the three-dimensional (3D) formation and evolution of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) shock waves and their role in plasma heating within a solar bipolar active region. Using 3D compressible, resistive MHD simulations, we model the emergence of magnetic flux from the convection zone into a magnetized corona. Our results reveal that initial plasmoid ejections launch hot plasma jets preceded by slow-mode shocks. Unlike established 2D models, these ejections originate from multiple sites along the emerging field's periphery, resulting in shocks with a complex, inverted-U 3D morphology. Beneath these fronts, the heated plasma forms flattened, sheet-like columns. Furthermore, we find that sustained gas pressure gradients, driven by dense plasma accumulation from plasmoids, power a cool, dense upflow adjacent to the main reconnection jet. During the main reconnection phase, the collision of ejected plasmoids with the ambient field triggers the formation of fast-mode termination shocks. By mapping viscous heating directly onto these irregular 3D shock surfaces, we demonstrate that energy dissipation is highly localized. This finding provides a physical link between shock-induced viscous heating and the observed temperature enhancements at the apex of post-flare loops.

title: Calculation of distant retrograde orbits and their use in space weather forecasting
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables, submitted to ApJ
summary: There is current renewed interest in using Sun-Earth distant retrograde orbits (DROs) for a space weather forecasting mission, which would temporarily place spacecraft at a position near the Sun-Earth line, but closer to the Sun than the L1 point (such as the ESA HENON mission and ESA SHIELD concept). With in situ observations of the magnetic field on a DRO, the southward ($B_z < 0$) magnetic field of interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs), which is not routinely accessible remotely, could be measured several hours in advance. This $B_z < 0$ field is a decisive factor for forecasting geomagnetic storm intensity. We present an analysis of DROs at different sub-L1 distances for their efficacy for a space weather forecasting mission. An open-source numerical framework to generate DRO trajectories is presented. Our pre-calculated orbits in Heliocentric Earth Ecliptic coordinates can be introduced into numerical or empirical simulations of the ambient solar wind and ICMEs. We then analyze the corresponding forecast lead times, the resulting observational gaps depending on the number of spacecraft and distance of a DRO, and the "cone of acceptance" of the maximum longitudinal separation of a spacecraft to the Sun-Earth line. We define different domains regarding radial evolution and longitudinal CME structure, and show the historical coverage of sub-L1 ICME observations with our ICMECAT catalog. An optimal mission configuration can be selected based on the characteristics of DROs presented here, depending on the requirements of such a mission deemed acceptable with respect to results on CME evolution and coherence.

title: An SRG/eROSITA Study of Be X-ray binaries in Quiescence
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Be X-ray binaries (BeXRBs) are mostly transient X-ray binaries with usually a neutron star as the compact object and a Be star as their optical companion. We performed a comprehensive analysis of BeXRBs in quiescence with the extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA), the soft X-ray instrument on board the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma satellite, using its first all-sky survey (eRASS1) data. The transient BeXRBs spend majority of time in their quiescent state, but are often studied during their outbursts. A quiescence study is useful to probe the emission mechanism of BeXRBs at low mass accretion rates. The spectra of BeXRBs detected in the eRASS1 main catalogue could be well fitted with a powerlaw as well as a blackbody model. In the absence of detection of a BeXRB, we report the luminosity upper limit for its position in the sky. The X-ray luminosity for the quiescent BeXRBs detected with eROSITA have $L_{X}\sim10^{33-36}$ erg s$^{-1}$ for both absorbed powerlaw and blackbody models in most cases. For the absorbed blackbody model, the emission seems to come from a fraction of the neutron star's surface. The quiescence luminosity of BeXRBs are used to distinguish between different accretion models at low mass accretion rates, like accretion in the propeller regime or from a cold accretion disc. The detection space of BeXRBs in quiescence for the eRASS1 data is compared against previously reported luminosities across multiple X-ray observatories.

title: NOCTURNE. VI. Hour-timescale radio variability in early-stage active galactic nucleus SDSS J122844.81+501751.2
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: Recently, a sample of radio-weak active galactic nuclei (AGN) was discovered to exhibit extreme Jy-level radio flares at 37~GHz. The origin of these extraordinary flares remains unknown. All sources host low-mass supermassive black holes, and most of them can be classified as narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. We employed multiwavelength observations to investigate one of these sources, SDSS J122844.81+501751.2, during a period of high 37~GHz activity. Our data include radio observations from Metsähovi Radio Observatory (MRO) at 37~GHz, OVRO at 15~GHz, and JVLA at 15, 22, and 33~GHz, as well as optical, UV, and X-ray observations from \textit{Swift}/XRT and UVOT. We studied the variability of the multiwavelength light curves (LC) using statistical tests, as well as derived the $e$-folding timescales of the flares. Utilising the timescales and the observed flare properties, we estimated the variability brightness temperatures and Doppler factors associated with the flares. Most individual LCs do not show statistically significant variability, which is likely due to the low number of measurements. The shortest timescale we estimated is only 1.1~hours, measured between MRO 37~GHz and JVLA 33~GHz detections. This is the fastest intrinsic radio variability reported in an AGN so far. This yielded an extreme variability brightness temperature of $T_\mathrm{B}$ = 4.20 $~\times$ 10$^{18}$~K and a variability Doppler factor of 438. We discuss magnetic eruptions near the black hole as a possible explanation for the extreme radio flares, and show that both incoherent and coherent processes can produce flares at these timescales. These flares challenge our current understanding of AGN radio variability. Whereas magnetic eruptions offer a viable explanation for the flares, more observations, preferably broadband and including polarisation, will be required to confirm their origin. (abridged)

title: A self-supervised machine learning approach to identify instrumental systematics in 21cm Cosmology
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures
summary: The primordial sound waves in the baryon-photon plasma are imprinted on the large-scale galaxy distribution as Baryon Acoustic Oscillations (BAO), serving as a cosmological standard ruler to constrain dark energy and the Hubble parameter. The upcoming 21cm intensity-mapping arrays are designed to map the 21cm emission across large volumes and measure the BAO scale. However, radio interferometers suffer from instrumental systematics that can hinder detection of the cosmological 21cm signal by leaking bright foregrounds into the signal-dominated modes. This work aims to demonstrate that a self-supervised model can predict the instrument systematic state (here, the amplitude of a spectral ripple in the beam width) in interferometric visibilities and potentially disentangle the instrument from the sky without a forward model. Based on the fact that an instrument stays the same as the sky rotates in a drift-scan observation, and that the same sky is observed under different instrument states, we train a convolutional autoencoder to compress the information in the simulated visibilities and separate this information into instrument-only and sky-only latent vectors. The result shows excellent prediction of the unknown instrument systematic for 15 held-out instrument states with $R^2 = 0.9975$ with a linear probe, against $R^2 = -3.55$ for a random-encoder baseline. The instrument-latent carries no detectable sky signal, as measured with a total-power sky proxy, for any held-out test data. The sky-latent vector and instrument-latent vector show partial separation but not complete disentanglement, identifying sky-latent purity as the primary open problem. The results show the ability of the model to recognize the systematic and show a promising path towards an ML-based foreground cleaning pipeline. Full instrument-sky disentanglement constitutes the natural next step.

title: Revealing the companion of NGC 1850-BH1
comment: Submitted to OJA
summary: The nature of the system NGC 1850-BH1 is discussed controversially in the literature. Located in the young (100 Myr) massive cluster NGC 1850 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, it was initially proposed to consist of a 5 $M_\odot$ main sequence turn-off star orbiting a stellar-mass black hole. However, subsequent analyses of the system have presented an alternative explanation, comprising of a lower mass (1-2 $M_\odot$) puffed-up donor star orbiting a rapidly rotating mass accretor. Efforts to discern the secondary's nature as a luminous star or a compact object in the original spectroscopy have remained inconclusive. In this work, we analyse a set of follow-up multi-epoch FLAMES-ARGUS spectra, which are bluer and of higher spectral resolution than the original data. Exploiting the spectral disentangling technique, we reveal the luminous secondary, and constrain the parameters of both components. We can describe the system self-consistently, adopting a 1.7 $\pm$ 0.4 $M_\odot$ puffed-up mass donor and a rapidly rotating ($v\sin{i} = 275$ km/s) 5.2 $\pm$ 2.6 $M_\odot$ luminous companion. While this rules out the black hole hypothesis, tensions with the analysis of the original data remain: Our inferred flux ratio of $\sim$ 35-50% in the red optical wavelength range is higher than the 10% upper limit found in previous work. The origin of this discrepancy remains unclear. Thanks to its location in a cluster of well-known mass and metallicity and its peculiar orbital properties, NGC 1850-BH1 has the potential to serve as a benchmark for mass-transfer efficiency studies.

title: A Hierarchical Bayesian Differential Calibration of the Gaia DR3 Parallax Zero Point Using Galactic Globular Clusters
summary: Globular clusters (GCs) occupy a broad range of stellar colors and magnitudes while sharing nearly the same distance. Gaia Data Release 3 parallaxes retain systematic zero-point residual variations for GCs, even after the correction by the widely used standard correction model (L21). We derive an empirical residual correction by the Hierarchical Bayesian Model, separating cluster-level offsets from the differential information carried by the member sequences. We first evaluate the L21 baseline at a fixed reference color, which assigns the remaining color-dependent correction to the residual model. Then we model the residual zero point, $δZ(G,ν_{\rm eff})$, with B-splines functions in color and magnitude--color interaction terms. The uncorrected cluster residuals exhibit a negative offset of approximately $25$--$40~μ{\rm as}$. The L21 baseline removes most of this offset but leaves coherent color- and magnitude-dependent structure. Applying the residual model brings the mean residuals close to zero, especially across most of the sampled color range. In five-fold cross-validation that excludes entire clusters from training, the correction modestly reduces the magnitude- and color-trend RMS relative to the L21 correction. The resulting model therefore provides a differential refinement of the \textit{Gaia} DR3 parallax zero-point within the calibrated domain for GCs, rather than an independent determination of its absolute value.

title: The First Deep Learning all-sky List of Fermi-LAT Gamma-ray Sources
summary:
Aims: We develop a deep-learning-based pipeline to construct a list of γ-ray sources and to quantitatively assess the impact of background uncertainties on source detection and characterization. This work extends and enhances the existing AutoSource-ID algorithm, previously adopted on optical observations, for applications on γ-ray data.
  Methods: Source detection was performed through image segmentation using a U-Net architecture, while dedicated deep neural networks (DNNs) were employed for source localization, flux estimation, and the classification of detected sources as either genuine or spurious. The training data were generated from Monte Carlo simulations based on 10 years of Fermi-LAT observations.
  Results: We present the first Fermi-LAT γ-ray all-sky source list derived using a deep-learning-based method (1FDL), containing more than 3800 sources with estimated positions, fluxes, and probability scores that quantify the likelihood of each detection being genuine or spurious. We further evaluated the robustness of the pipeline against variations in the interstellar emission model (IEM) and compared the resulting source list with the 4FGL-DR2 catalog.
  Conclusion: We find that the our deep-learning-based approach achieves performance comparable to, or better than, the likelihood-based methods employed in the standard Fermi-LAT catalog pipeline when tested against changes in the IEM. The 1FDL source list is broadly consistent with the Fermi-LAT 4FGL-DR2 catalog obtained over the same 10-year observational period, including a few new sources confirmed in the recent Fermi-LAT 16-year source list (FL16Y). These results demonstrate the potential of DNN methods for the detection and characterization of γ-ray sources and provide a foundation for their application in future high-energy astrophysical analyses.

title: Impact of Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus Debris on Milky Way Escape-velocity Estimates in TNG50
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: The escape velocity is a key probe of the Milky Way (MW) potential, but standard estimates can be biased by unrelaxed substructures. Using MW analogs from the TNG50 cosmological simulation, we investigate the impact of the dominant, highly radial Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) debris on escape-velocity measurements. We introduce an adaptive selection strategy that balances statistical reliability with sample size to identify the power-law decline regime of the local halo velocity distribution. Applying this strategy to 16 MW analogs with prominent GSE-like structures and continuous high-velocity tails, we find that retaining GSE-like stars yields a systematic underestimate, with a recovery fraction of $97.5^{+2.1}_{-2.9}\%$, while removing GSE-like stars alone increases the recovery fraction to $99.4^{+2.1}_{-2.5}\%$. The $\sim 2\%$ underestimation of the escape velocity corresponds to an $\sim 6\%$ underestimation of the total mass. This improvement persists in LAMOST-like magnitude and footprint selection. GSE-like debris is therefore a key contributor to the systematic underestimation of escape-velocity measurements, with direct implications for the inferred MW mass.

title: Cosmological Constraints on Interacting Dark Matter with SPT-3G D1
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures
summary: Models of the dark sector in which the dark matter participates in nontrivial interactions can create detectable signatures in cosmological observables, providing non-terrestrial means of probing the nature of dark matter. In this work, we test dark matter-baryon scattering, dark matter-dark radiation interactions, and dark matter annihilation using measurements of the CMB and BAO. We leverage the latest SPT-3G D1 CMB measurements of the primary anisotropies, alongside the D1 MUSE lensing data, to set up-to-date bounds on these models. From the combination of Planck, ACT DR6, and SPT-3G D1 data, we constrain the velocity-independent dark matter-baryon scattering cross-section to $σ_\mathrm{DM-b} < 4.6\times10^{-26}~\mathrm{cm^2}$, the dark matter-dark radiation momentum transfer rate to $Γ_\mathrm{0,nadm}<5.2\times10^{-8}\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$, and the effective dark matter annihilation parameter, quantifying the fractional thermally averaged cross-section, to $p_\mathrm{ann}<3.7\times10^{-28}~\mathrm{cm^3/s/GeV}$, all at the 95% confidence level. The improved sensitivity to the first two models is in particular driven by the precision measurements of CMB lensing at small scales provided by SPT-3G D1 MUSE lensing data. For annihilating dark matter, due to the degeneracy of the effect with the optical depth to reionization, we observe a non-trivial relationship between the upper bound on $p_\mathrm{ann}$ and the large-scale polarization information. When combining CMB data with the latest measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), upper bounds on extended model parameters can appear to tighten as the model space attempts to accommodate the known discrepancy between these data. Future CMB and BAO measurements will provide better clarity on reconciling this discrepancy and enhance our ability to test dark matter interactions.

title: The Clouds in the "Middle Ages" I. Star formation history and chemical abundances in the LMC
comment: 13 pages, 13 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: The LMC is a benchmark galaxy for studying stellar evolution, chemical enrichment, and galaxy interactions due to its proximity and intermediate metallicity. While its star formation history (SFH) has been extensively studied using colour-magnitude diagram (CMD) fitting techniques and the chemical enrichment is largely based on red giant branch (RGB) stars, the asymptotic giant branch (AGB) population - a key tracer of intermediate-ages - has received less attention in these analyses. We aim to reconstruct the SFH of the LMC using AGB stars and to study their reliability as tracers of chemical abundances. The initial sample of 879 AGB stars from the Gaia DR3 long-period variable catalog was extended to 2047 fundamental-mode pulsators by applying separate O-rich and C-rich period-Wesenheit relations; OGLE-III cross-matching then showed that only 256 of these stars are Mira variables. We reconstructed the SFH using two period-age calibrations: the theoretical relation of Trabucchi and Mowlavi (2022) and the empirical calibration of Zhang and Sanders (2023). For the chemical abundance analysis, we used APOGEE DR17 spectra for 296 AGB and 271 RGB stars, applying a refined line-by-line abundance pipeline with a tailored line selection to derive Mg, Si, and Ca abundances. The two calibrations yield significantly different SFHs, and neither matches independent CMD-based results equally well, so we present both rather than one fiducial choice. Our SFH reveals three distinct phases: an ancient population at 9-10 Gyr, a quiescent phase at 4-8 Gyr, and a starburst peaking at 1.5-2 Gyr. Our chemical analysis demonstrates that carefully selected Mg, Si, and Ca lines yield significantly reduced intrinsic scatter compared to APOGEE DR17 results. AGB stars prove to be reliable tracers of both the SFH and chemical enrichment of the LMC, provided that careful line selection and calibration are applied.

title: Revisiting the Photometric Modulation Amplitudes of Kepler Planet Hosts: A Confounder-Adjusted Test of Stellar Spin-Orbit Alignment
comment: 21 pages, 11 figures, accepted for publication in AJ
summary: T. Mazeh and coworkers pioneered a method using rotational photometric modulation as a proxy to infer stellar obliquities in Kepler transiting planetary systems, based on the expected positive correlation between spot-induced modulation amplitudes and stellar inclinations. They found that planet hosts cooler than the Sun showed larger modulation amplitudes than comparison stars, consistent with low stellar obliquities. For hotter hosts, however, they reported the opposite - a negative amplitude difference (hosts minus comparison stars) - which is difficult to interpret in terms of viewing geometry. We show that this comparison is affected by confounding variables not controlled for in the sample selection. One such confounder is apparent magnitude, whose distributions differ markedly between the two samples for hotter stars and affect the observed modulation amplitudes. We develop resampling and likelihood-based approaches that enable comparison of the amplitude distributions at fixed apparent magnitude, stellar radius, and rotation period. The previously reported negative amplitude difference for hot hosts is no longer present in either analysis. The likelihood-based analysis finds a positive amplitude difference up to $\sim 6100\,\mathrm{K}$ that becomes consistent with zero at higher temperatures, while the resampling analysis shows a similar but less pronounced trend. This result is qualitatively consistent with independent $v\sin i$ analyses suggesting low obliquities for cooler super-Earth and sub-Neptune hosts and broader obliquity distributions for hotter ones. This may also indicate a gradual change in the obliquity distribution with stellar temperature, although changes in spot distributions or selection effects could also contribute to the photometric trends in hot stars.

title: $γ$-ray variability of changing-look blazars: FSRQ-like jet behaviour
comment: 18 pages, 15 figures, Submitted
summary: Changing-look blazars (CLBs) move between the flat-spectrum radio quasar (FSRQ) and BL Lacertae (BL Lac) optical classifications. Either the accretion flow switches regime, or a brightening jet continuum swamps the broad lines while the system itself is unchanged. The two pictures predict the same optical behaviour but differ in the jet, so the $γ$-ray emission could potentially separate them. Catalogue quantities averaged over the mission cannot, because a permanently intermediate source and one alternating between two states return the same mean. We therefore use 17.9\,yr of \textit{Fermi}-LAT light curves at 3-, 7- and 30-day cadence, comparing CLBs with BL Lac and FSRQ controls selected and analysed identically. CLBs and FSRQs have indistinguishable fractional variability, with medians of 0.483 and 0.437 at 30-day cadence ($p = 0.94$), while BL Lacs are far less variable at 0.262 ($p = 1.4\times10^{-4}$). The result survives restricting the controls to low-synchrotron-peaked sources and matching in flux and sampling. Several further diagnostics group CLBs with FSRQs, as does their Eddington-scaled disc luminosity. Followed through time, CLB light curves show no excess of bimodal flux distributions, and the direction of the optical transition does not predict how the $γ$-ray spectrum evolves. CLBs do reach hard, BL Lac-like spectra more often than FSRQs, but never for longer than chance allows. Only in this, and in how their spectra respond to brightening, do they fall between the two classes. The changing-look phenomenon therefore leaves little imprint on the $γ$-ray jet, favouring a variable jet continuum over a change of accretion regime.

title: ASKAP Discovery of a Giant Odd Radio Circle at $z=0.15$
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables
summary: Odd radio circles (ORCs) are a recently recognized class of faint, roughly circular diffuse radio sources, typically a few hundred kiloparsecs across, whose origin is still debated. We report the serendipitous discovery of a giant ORC, ORC~J1928$-$5056, in 856~MHz continuum data from the ASKAP observations. The emission forms a single, mildly elliptical structure $4^{\prime}$ across, corresponding to $0.63$~Mpc at the redshift $z=0.1507$ of the central galaxy LEDA~140850, the brightest cluster galaxy of Abell~3639, which makes it one of the largest single ORCs known. After subtracting the radio nucleus associated with the host galaxy, the ORC has a flux density of 73~mJy integrated within an area of $\sim 12$~arcmin$^2$, i.e.\ a mean surface brightness of only $1.7$~$μ$Jy~arcsec$^{-2}$, and a rest-frame luminosity of $L_{1.4}=2\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, comparable to those of the most luminous ORCs. Including its nucleus, the system reaches $L_{1.4}=6.6\times10^{24}$~W~Hz$^{-1}$, higher than that of any other ORC reported so far. The host is a massive ($M_{\ast}\sim10^{11}\,M_{\odot}$), passive elliptical galaxy with negligible star formation. It contains an AGN jet with a power-law spectrum of index $α=-0.877\pm0.089$ between 856 and 1656~MHz. Finally, we discuss the implications for ORC formation models and the observations needed to establish the nature of this system.

title: Improving cosmological distance measurements at high redshift using Lyman-Alpha forest BAO reconstruction
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures
summary: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) measures baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) in the Lyman-$α$ (Lyman-alpha) forest and provides a robust probe of the expansion history in the matter-dominated era. Yet, non-linear structure formation broadens and shifts the BAO peak. To undo these effects, we extend standard Zel'dovich reconstruction, routinely applied to galaxy surveys, to the Lyman-alpha forest. We validate our methodology on large-volume idealized Lyman-alpha forest mocks painted on top of the \textsc{AbacusSummit} $N$-body simulations, using linear control variates to suppress sample variance and thereby reduce the error bars by a factor of up to $\approx \sqrt{50}$. In fully sampled periodic boxes, reconstruction halves the radial BAO damping scale and reduces the uncertainties on the radial ($\apar$) and transverse ($\aperp$) scaling parameters by $\approx25\%$ and $\approx15\%$, respectively. It also reduces the non-linear shift from $Δ\apar=+0.3\%$ to $+0.10\pm0.07\%$, while $\aperp$ remains unbiased. To make this approach readily applicable to observational data, we demonstrate the impact of a survey mask with a DESI-like density of $50\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. For this mask, we compare two approaches to estimate the displacement field: either directly from the Lyman-alpha forest or using an external tracer with a number density of $\bar n \simeq 10^{-3}\,h^3\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, such as Lyman-break galaxies and Lyman-$α$ emitters---both key targets for DESI-II. Both approaches give comparable gains and reduce the uncertainties on $\apar$ and $\aperp$ by $\approx 27\%$ and $\approx 10\%$, respectively, with mild improvements for futuristic high-density surveys with $160\,\mathrm{deg}^{-2}$. Correspondingly, the figure of merit improves by factors of $1.66$ for fully sampled boxes, $1.65$ for a DESI-like, and $1.76$ for a high-density survey.

title: The dearth of dustless HdC stars in the Magellanic Clouds: A metallicity-driven white dwarf merger mass effect
comment: 17 pages, 20 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Hydrogen-deficient carbon (HdC) stars are rare supergiants believed to form through the merger of two white dwarfs (WDs). They comprise the dust-producing R Coronae Borealis (RCB) stars and the dustless HdC (dLHdC) stars. While dedicated Galactic surveys find the two subclasses in roughly equal numbers, no dLHdC star had previously been identified in the Magellanic Clouds, despite 30 known RCB stars in these two galaxies. We present the first systematic search for dLHdC stars in the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, aiming to measure the dLHdC-to-RCB ratio in environments of distinct metallicities and well-constrained star formation histories. Candidates were selected from the Gaia DR3 Magellanic catalogue using colour-magnitude cuts combining Gaia, SkyMapper DR4, and VMC DR6 photometry, complemented by a random-forest classifier trained on known Galactic dLHdC stars. The search reached an overall detection efficiency of ~96%. All candidates were followed up spectroscopically with WiFeS on the ANU 2.3m telescope. We discovered the first two Magellanic dLHdC stars: SP77 29-5 in the LMC and SMSS 005551.43-723139.2 in the SMC, the latter belonging to the rare Sr-rich subclass. The resulting dLHdC-to-RCB number ratio of ~1:15 overall is far below the near-unity Galactic value. We argue this deficit is intrinsic rather than observational. Convolving the delay time distribution from a sub-class of white dwarf mergers with each Cloud's star formation history, we estimate that ~80% (LMC) and about two-thirds (SMC) of HdC stars originate from mergers with short delay times, which at low metallicity are biased towards higher total WD masses, and thus towards the luminous regime associated with RCB stars rather than the fainter dLHdC population.

title: The First Deep Learning all-sky List of Fermi-LAT Gamma-ray Sources
summary:
Aims: We develop a deep-learning-based pipeline to construct a list of γ-ray sources and to quantitatively assess the impact of background uncertainties on source detection and characterization. This work extends and enhances the existing AutoSource-ID algorithm, previously adopted on optical observations, for applications on γ-ray data.
  Methods: Source detection was performed through image segmentation using a U-Net architecture, while dedicated deep neural networks (DNNs) were employed for source localization, flux estimation, and the classification of detected sources as either genuine or spurious. The training data were generated from Monte Carlo simulations based on 10 years of Fermi-LAT observations.
  Results: We present the first Fermi-LAT γ-ray all-sky source list derived using a deep-learning-based method (1FDL), containing more than 3800 sources with estimated positions, fluxes, and probability scores that quantify the likelihood of each detection being genuine or spurious. We further evaluated the robustness of the pipeline against variations in the interstellar emission model (IEM) and compared the resulting source list with the 4FGL-DR2 catalog.
  Conclusion: We find that the our deep-learning-based approach achieves performance comparable to, or better than, the likelihood-based methods employed in the standard Fermi-LAT catalog pipeline when tested against changes in the IEM. The 1FDL source list is broadly consistent with the Fermi-LAT 4FGL-DR2 catalog obtained over the same 10-year observational period, including a few new sources confirmed in the recent Fermi-LAT 16-year source list (FL16Y). These results demonstrate the potential of DNN methods for the detection and characterization of γ-ray sources and provide a foundation for their application in future high-energy astrophysical analyses.

title: Impact of Neutrino Trapping on the Equation of State and Structure of Hybrid Stars with 2SC Quark Matter
summary: We investigate how sensitive the effects of neutrino trapping on hot hybrid stars are to uncertainties in the hadronic and quark equations of state and in the thermodynamic construction of the hadron--quark transition. The hadronic phase is described by finite-temperature covariant density functional equations of state, and the quark phase by a three-flavor Nambu--Jona-Lasinio (NJL) model with repulsive vector interactions and two-flavor color superconductivity. Because confinement is absent from the NJL model, an effective pressure shift $B^*$ is used phenomenologically to locate the deconfinement transition. We construct isentropic stellar equations of state with and without trapped electron neutrinos, vary the quark vector coupling and the nuclear symmetry-energy slope, and compare global with local conservation of electron-lepton number within phase coexistence. Neutrino trapping generically shifts deconfinement toward higher density throughout the parameter range considered. Increasing the vector interaction stiffens quark matter and raises the maximum stellar mass, but only moderately for the couplings studied. We also examine stronger diquark pairing and RG-consistent regularization, instead of sharp momentum cut-off: both affect the pairing gap, phase boundaries, and quark-core composition more strongly than they alter the qualitative trends of the stellar mass--radius sequences. Conversely, trapping reduces the sensitivity to the hadronic symmetry-energy slope because the enhanced proton fraction drives matter toward greater isospin symmetry. Global and local lepton-number prescriptions produce rather similar mass--radius relations but substantially different internal phase structures: global conservation leads to a considerably more extended mixed phase.

title: A Hierarchical Bayesian Differential Calibration of the Gaia DR3 Parallax Zero Point Using Galactic Globular Clusters
summary: Globular clusters (GCs) occupy a broad range of stellar colors and magnitudes while sharing nearly the same distance. Gaia Data Release 3 parallaxes retain systematic zero-point residual variations for GCs, even after the correction by the widely used standard correction model (L21). We derive an empirical residual correction by the Hierarchical Bayesian Model, separating cluster-level offsets from the differential information carried by the member sequences. We first evaluate the L21 baseline at a fixed reference color, which assigns the remaining color-dependent correction to the residual model. Then we model the residual zero point, $δZ(G,ν_{\rm eff})$, with B-splines functions in color and magnitude--color interaction terms. The uncorrected cluster residuals exhibit a negative offset of approximately $25$--$40~μ{\rm as}$. The L21 baseline removes most of this offset but leaves coherent color- and magnitude-dependent structure. Applying the residual model brings the mean residuals close to zero, especially across most of the sampled color range. In five-fold cross-validation that excludes entire clusters from training, the correction modestly reduces the magnitude- and color-trend RMS relative to the L21 correction. The resulting model therefore provides a differential refinement of the \textit{Gaia} DR3 parallax zero-point within the calibrated domain for GCs, rather than an independent determination of its absolute value.

title: The SIRMOS mission concept: a space-based near-IR spectroscopic survey of 100 million galaxies in the Euclid Wide Survey footprint
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 6 tables, presented at SPIE Space Telescopes and Instrumentation 2026: Optical, Infrared, and Millimeter Wave (August 2026)
summary:
SIRMOS is a mission concept for a future NASA Astrophysics Explorer opportunity that aims to revolutionize our understanding of the universe by mapping the large-scale structure of galaxies in unprecedented breadth and detail to explore cosmic origins and evolution. Specifically, the primary science goals of SIRMOS are to discover how cosmic inflation seeded large-scale structure, reveal the nature of the accelerating expansion of the universe, and measure the sum of neutrino masses to exceptionally high precision. Its secondary science goals include determining how environment shapes galaxy evolution at cosmic noon and beyond, and probing the Milky Way's dust-enshrouded regions, reaching the far side of our Galaxy.
  To accomplish its transformative science goals, SIRMOS executes a 3-year cosmology survey over the Euclid footprint of ~14,000 deg$^2$, obtaining slit spectra for ~100 million galaxies at 1<z<4. SIRMOS is the first space mission designed specifically to leverage Euclid's wide near-infrared (IR) imaging survey for target selection and employs a digital micro-mirror device (DMD) to acquire up to 4,000 simultaneous spectra over a wide 0.9 deg$^2$ field of view. The instrument's excellent spectral resolution of $R=1300$ and continuous wavelength coverage from 1.25--2.5 $μ$m capture the redshifts of distant galaxies with no gaps, reducing systematic biases to achieve ground-breaking science.

title: Absence of Magnetic Suppression in Massive Star Variability
comment: To submit to AAS Journals. Comments welcome!
summary: Although stochastic low-frequency (SLF) variability is ubiquitous among hot, massive stars, its physical origin remains uncertain. One proposed explanation is that this variability is produced by internal gravity waves (IGWs) excited in the stellar interior by convection in the stellar core or subsurface layers. Strong magnetic fields, however, are expected to significantly attenuate such waves. In this work, we model the conditions for magnetic gravity-wave suppression in 17 magnetic hot stars that exhibit significant SLF variability. We find that in many cases, IGWs excited at frequencies comparable to the observed variability should be strongly suppressed by the magnetic field, sometimes across a substantial fraction of the frequency range containing the observed SLF power. This finding challenges IGWs as a universal explanation for SLF variability in massive stars and motivates the consideration of alternative origins.

title: Neglecting Dynamical Microlensing Can Bias Accretion Disk Size Measurements at the Population Level
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables
summary: Microlensing of strongly lensed quasars probes unresolved accretion disks, but many inference methods use static magnification maps with fixed relative microlens positions. Using the GPU-accelerated simulator Microcaustics, we generate ten-year multiband light curves for three quadruply lensed quasar configurations. We compare dynamical microlensing with independent microlens motions against coherent bulk motion, and a microlens mass distribution against equal masses, keeping the velocity distribution of individual microlenses and mean mass fixed. We infer population disk sizes using ridge regression on the means and lower and upper scatters of ten variability and event metrics. We measure biases by applying models trained with simplified physics to simulations including both effects. Models trained on coherent motion interpret the additional variability from evolving caustics as smaller disks. For populations of 128 independent realizations, jointly inferred radii are consistently smaller by 6-28%. Microlens dynamics increase caustic-crossing rates pooled across all four macroimages by 5-15% and r-band high-magnification-event (HME) rates by 13-25%, while shortening median HME durations by 4-12%. Omitting the mass distribution produces configuration-dependent disk-size offsets from -12% to +5%. Including the mass distribution decreases caustic-crossing rates by 6-8% and HME rates by 6-12%. It also narrows the spread of ten-year averaged microlensing time-delay differences between macroimages by a median of 9-12% per system, while microlens dynamics have a smaller, image-pair-dependent effect. These results demonstrate the importance of microlens dynamics for population disk-size inference and motivate simulations that include dynamical microlensing and a microlens mass distribution.

title: Probing the inner disk edge of rotating neutron stars with dipole excitations in finite nuclei
comment: 4 pages, 3 figures
summary: The nuclear equation of state shapes both the structure of rapidly rotating neutron stars and the orbital motion in their surrounding spacetime. Its uncertainty affects the mass and radius at which the innermost stable circular orbit reaches the stellar surface, a condition that defines the transition between disks whose inner edge is set by the surface and those truncated by orbital instability. We quantify how measurements of the electric dipole polarizability of neutron-rich nuclei reduce the uncertainty in this transition and in the orbital properties at the disk inner edge. We compute uniformly rotating neutron stars in general relativity for a family of equations of state that systematically vary the symmetry energy, derived from relativistic energy density functionals with density-dependent point-coupling interactions. We compare the results for the full family with those for the subset consistent with the measured dipole polarizabilities of finite nuclei. The dipole polarizability constraint reduces the spread in transition mass and equatorial radius by factors of about seven to ten across the spin frequencies considered. Along this transition, it also confines the orbital frequency at the disk inner edge to a band narrower than $20$~Hz at each spin. Combined with a measured neutron-star spin, a kilohertz quasi-periodic oscillation interpreted as disk orbital motion further restricts the mass--radius region, allowing an independent mass estimate to probe the symmetry-energy constraint. The dipole response of finite nuclei thus informs both the structure of rotating neutron stars and the orbital properties of their inner accretion disks.

title: A Collimated Protostellar Outflow Likely Driven by Jet and Reshaped by Environment in the Sagittarius C Cloud of the Central Molecular Zone
comment: Submitted to ApJ
summary: The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) at the center of the Galaxy provides a nearby laboratory for studying star formation under extreme physical and chemical conditions. Recent ALMA (Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array) observations have identified 43 candidate protostellar outflows in three CMZ clouds. One of these, the Sgr C-F#2 outflow in Sagittarius C (Sgr C), has a highly collimated lobe extending approximately 0.8 pc in projection. Here we present a joint analysis of ALMA observations of SiO J=8-7, 5-4, and 2-1. We use local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) and non-LTE methods to constrain the SiO column densities, H2 number density, and gas temperature. The low SiO rotational temperatures and higher kinetic temperatures inferred from non-LTE methods suggest subthermal excitation. The elongated SiO morphology, shock-excited gas, position-velocity structure, and the alignment of the red shifted molecular lobe with JWST infrared knots altogether favor jet-dominated entrainment, whereas a broader disk-wind component close to the source cannot be excluded. The outflow shows asymmetries in its morphology and physical properties, which can be attributed to dense gas on the path of its lobe impeding its propagation and feedback from a nearby HII region imposing different pressure on its two sides.

title: Prospects for Near-Far Constraints on Reionization from Simulated LSST Observations of Milky Way Dwarf Galaxies and Stellar Streams
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, submitted to ApJ. Data available at http://app.globus.org/file-manager?origin_id=fef57d95-ed3b-430f-a4a3-132a95d83a00
summary: The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) will detect resolved stellar populations of intact dwarf galaxies and disrupted stellar streams in the Milky Way (MW) halo and beyond, opening a new avenue for near-field cosmology, particularly for constraining the faint galaxies during reionization. To interpret these data, we present and publicly release mock LSST catalogs of satellites, stellar streams, phase-mixed galaxies, and field galaxies around 13 MW-mass hosts in the FIRE-2 zoom-in simulations, generated with \textsf{py-ananke}. Using a surface brightness limit of $μ_{g} \leq 34$ $\rm{mag}$ $\rm{arcsec^{-2}}$, we find that $\approx29\%$ of streams with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 5 \times 10^5$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable with tidal tails, while another $\approx38\%$ are detectable only through their bound progenitors and would appear as satellites. We estimate that $\approx96\%$ of satellites and $\approx64\%$ of field galaxies (out to $\sim$3.5 Mpc) with $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{5}$ $M_{\odot}$ are detectable, decreasing to $\approx$59\% and $\approx$42\% for $M_{\star} \gtrsim 10^{4.5}$ $M_{\odot}$ owing to resolution limits. Including streams detectable as satellites reproduces the radial distribution of observed MW satellites, suggesting that some observed satellites may be bound remnants of disrupted systems. Our mock galaxies match the sizes of observed satellites with $M_{\rm{V}} \lesssim -6$. Star-formation histories computed from only the detectable stars broadly recover the simulated star-formation histories. As an application, we test the near-far technique for reconstructing the proto-MW ultraviolet luminosity function (UVLF) during reionization ($z \gtrsim 6$). Adding the detectable streams improves the recovered faint-end slope at $z = 7$ and reduces the halo-to-halo scatter by $\approx33\%$.

title: Evidence for a nova super-remnant surrounding the recurrent nova V745 Scorpii using eROSITA
comment: 13 pages, 10 figures; Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Nova super-remnants (NSRs) are vast shell-like structures encompassing recurrent novae (RNe), created through the excavation of large amounts of local interstellar medium by repeated nova eruptions. Simulations predict that such NSRs should surround all novae.
